## Methods

Animals
All experimental procedures were performed in accordance with the guidelines of and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at KAIST (approval number No. KA2024-007-v4). Wild-type C57BL/6J male and female mice were used in the behavioral studies. The mice were group-housed for the first week at 7 weeks of age and then transferred at 8 weeks of age to separate cages under a 12-h light-dark cycle (light on from 8:00 to 20:00) at room temperature (22°C) and 40% humidity to allow them to accommodate to the housing facility. We used mice from at least three litters, and mice were randomly allocated into groups to balance potential genetic or developmental variance. Food and water were provided ad libitum.

Mouse models for depressive-like behavior
Chronic unpredictable stress (CUS) model. Wild-type C57BL/6 male or female mice (8-week-old) were subjected to nine different stressors: (i) 24 h of food and water deprivation, (ii) 8 h of cage tilting (45°), (iii) 24 h of light cycle reversal, (iv) 5 min of swimming in cold water (13±1°C), (v) 2 min of tail pinching 1 cm from the end of the tail, (vi) 8 h of moist bedding, (vii) 30 min of cold exposure (4°C), (viii) 12 h of sleep deprivation with a cylindrical pedestal (2.5 cm diameter and 3 cm height) placed on the cage floor filled with 1 cm-deep tap water to prevent the sleep during dark phase, and (ix) 1 h of physical restraint. These stressors were randomly scheduled over four weeks, with one or two stressors performed daily in a random combination to magnify unpredictability. During the test week (week 4), we omitted the cold swimming and tail pinching to prevent repetitive exposure and habituation effects. In periodic assessments of depressive-like behaviors, behavioral tests (TST and FST) were conducted at the beginning of each week, while forced swimming and tail-pinch stressors were excluded from the CUS paradigm to avoid confounding effects. Control mice were individually housed for four weeks with short daily handling in the housing room. We measured the mouse body weight each week at a fixed time during depressive-like behavior induction. Experimental batches and the number of mice per batch are listed in the Supplementary Table 4.

Lipopolysaccharide-induced mouse model. LPS (serotype O55:B5, Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: L2880) was freshly prepared on the test day by dissolving in sterile 0.9% NaCl solution (normal saline). The solution was administered to 8-week-old male C57BL/6 mice with an intraperitoneal injection (i.p.) at a volume of 0.1 ml per mouse. The dose of LPS (0.83 mg/kg) was selected based on the meta-analysis for experimental studies on inflammation-associated depressive-like behavior, which is known to elicit the full spectrum of acute sickness behaviors39, including physiological and behavioral changes relevant to depressive-like phenotypes40. Control animals received an equivalent volume of sterile saline.

Corticosterone-induced mouse model. Eight-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned to three groups and received the following administration protocol: (i) corticosterone (20 mg/kg, Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: D27840) for consecutive 21 days, (ii) vehicle (normal saline containing 0.1% dimethyl sulfoxide and 0.1% Tween-80) for consecutive 21 days, or (iii) vehicle for 14 days followed by corticosterone for 7 days. All injections were delivered subcutaneously once daily at a volume of 5 ml kg−1 body weight27,41.

Behavioral studies
AVATAR studio recording. All mice were handled in the behavior room for 10 min per day for 3 consecutive days and habituated to the room for an hour before the behavioral experiments. AVATAR studio consists of an opaque hemispheric chamber with five recording cameras (Full-HD CMOS, 1200×1200 pixels, 30 frames per second) and an LED light device (20 lux) at the bottom23. An open field apparatus, 5-mm-thick transparent acrylic panels (20 cm×20 cm×30 cm), is located at the center of the AVATAR studio. The mice were placed in the center of the chamber and allowed to freely explore the apparatus for 20 min. For the investigation of individual variance, we conducted recordings a day before the induction of a depressive-like state model. To estimate the effects of CUS on exploratory behaviors, the mice were recorded a day after exposure to the last stressor. From the video, the 3D coordination of nine key body points (nose, head, anus, tail tip, torso, left and right hind limb, left and right forelimb) was calculated from multiple 2D images following a computer-vision 3D calibration and reconstruction algorithm, which calculates the intersection of the ray from the optical center of the camera through anatomical landmarks for a given camera arrangement42. The obtained 3D coordinate parameters were processed to generate joint connections for the formation of the action skeleton, a vectorial representation of body configuration in 3D space, on both allocentric and egocentric coordinate systems. The accuracy of AVATARnet for keypoint prediction was evaluated using three standard metrics: Area of Overlap (IoU), Average Precision (AP), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE). AVATARnet achieved IoU consistently above 75% across nine anatomical key points and mAP values around 90% after sufficient network training. The positional error, measured as MSE, ranged from 7 to 15 pixels, equivalent to 1.4–4.5 mm in physical space, and the average RMSE recorded 10.19 pixels, corresponding to approximately 2–3 mm23.

Sucrose preference test. For habituation, we provided mice with two bottles, one containing 1% sucrose (Sigma, Cat# S7903) solution and the other containing regular water alone, for 48 h before the sucrose preference test (SPT). We changed the left-right position of the bottles every 24 h in the adaptation phase to avoid any location preference. In the formal experiment, mice were allowed to freely access the 1% sucrose and water bottles for 24 h with food withholding. The positions of the bottles were switched after 12 h of testing to exclude the potential effects of side preference. After the test, we moved the mice to the home cage and measured the total intake of each fluid. Sucrose preference was calculated as follows: sucrose preference (%) = 100 × sucrose consumption (g) / (sucrose + water consumption) (g). A minimal layer of sawdust was added to each cage to detect any bottle leakage.

Tail suspension test. Mice were suspended from a stick by their tails 50 cm above the ground for six minutes. The sticky tape was used to attach the stick to a spot 1 cm from the end of the tail41. We recorded video from the side and measured the immobility duration during 6 min of suspension using a video tracking system (Smart 3.0). Mice were considered immobile when hanging motionless, swinging passively, or remaining completely motionless.

Forced swimming test. The forced swimming test (FST) was conducted to assess the behavioral effect of stress exposure, at least four hours after the TST to minimize any potential effect of physical discomfort caused by tail suspension. A clear glass cylinder (20 cm height, 12 cm diameter) was filled to a depth of 15 cm with water (24±1°C) to prevent any physical contact of the tail or hind limbs with the bottom of the container. Mice were placed in a water-filled cylinder for six minutes. Video was recorded from the side with a web camera recording system and monitored using a video tracking system (Smart 3.0). We only quantified the duration of immobility during the final four minutes in an observer-blinded manner, as most mice move around at the beginning of the FST43. We defined immobility as the status in which mice floated (motionless) or merely moved their paws to maintain balance in the water.

Time in the center and moving distance. We extracted the time spent in the arena center and the distance traveled from the AVATAR studio recording videos to measure the locomotive function of mice. In 20-min sessions, we measured the time mice stayed in the center square of the open field (10×10 cm) and the total distance traveled by tracking the x- and y-axis coordinates of the body center.

Pharmacological treatment of animals
Monoaminergic antidepressants. Male or female 10-week-old C57BL/6J mice were used to investigate the effects of monoaminergic antidepressants on free exploratory behaviors. All drugs were dissolved in sterile 0.9% NaCl solution (normal saline) and injected intraperitoneally for 14 consecutive days. For both fluoxetine hydrochloride (Abcam, Cat#: ab120077) and imipramine hydrochloride (Abcam, Cat#: ab141046), 15 mg kg−1 was dissolved in 200 µl of vehicle. Control mice were only injected with the vehicle (normal saline). For all behavioral experiments, mice were tested 24 h after the final injection.

Non-monoaminergic antidepressants. Non-monoaminergic antidepressants were administered to 12-week-old male C57BL/6J mice exposed to chronic stress for four weeks. Agmatine sulfate salt (50 mg kg−1, Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: A7127)44, scopolamine hydrobromide (0.5 mg kg−1, Tocris Bioscience, Cat#: 1414)45,46, and Rapastinel (or GLYX-13) (10 mg kg−1, Tocris Bioscience, Cat#: 3406)47 were dissolved in 0.9% saline and injected intraperitoneally at a volume of 5 ml kg−1 body weight, 24 h before behavioral experiments.

Manual label assignment and cluster annotation
We established a mouse behavior database for the evaluation of our machine learning framework. Thirteen different behavior labels were assigned to each frame of a 20-min video of a freely moving mouse. Coarse behavior phenotypes were defined according to the Mouse Ethogram database taxonomy (www.mousebehavior.org). We further concretized these coarse labels with fine-grained labels to provide more detailed discrimination of the spontaneous motions of well-known behavior sequences (Supplementary Table 2). After this process, each annotated behavior segment contained information about the start/end frame number and a single fine-grained label. To annotate the unsupervised learning-driven clusters with behavior components, experts explored twenty corresponding video clips for each cluster and determined if the behavior sequences in the video clip could be associated with fine-grained labels. The behavior labels that appeared in the video clip were scored and averaged as part of a numerical evaluation of cluster characteristics. We then summarized the features of the behavioral phenotypes (a maximum of two) with more subtle descriptions.

CLOSER Framework
Data augmentation. Contrastive learning requires an appropriate data augmentation strategy to maximize the performance of the machine learning model. We introduced four augmentation methods: “Scale”, “ChangeStartPoint”, “ChangeAngle”, and “ChannelMask”. “Scale” is accomplished by random scaling of the original mouse 3D skeleton vector size by a factor of 0.5 to 1.5. For the given motion sequence fi = {xi, yi, zi}t, the augmented motion sequence was defined as Scale(fi) = α{xi, yi, zi}t, while 0.5 ≤ α ≤ 1.5. Scale enables the model to learn the irrelevance of mouse size in its behavior. “ChangeStartPoint” simulates the temporal heterogeneity of behavior sequences that originates in variations in the duration of the motion segments. To accomplish this, we randomly cropped 60% of the original motion sequence and then performed a linear interpolation to the original length according to this relationship: ChangeStartPoint fi 1...T = Interpolate fi s::e, 1 ≤ s, e ≤ T, e-s+1 = 0.6 × T. We employed “ChangeAngle” to distort the angle between the skeleton vectors of a chosen joint and its parent skeleton vectors with a maximum distortion of 1.75 radians. Three joints were selected randomly. The angles between the skeleton vectors v involving the chosen joints and their parent skeleton vectors v were calculated using the following equation: θ = acos (v1·v2 / |v1||v2|); θnew = θ + Δ, -30° ≤ Δ ≤ 30°. For the investigation of new cartesian coordinates X, we built a linear system as follows: Concat(n, v1, v2) X = Concat(P v1 + |v2| |v1| cos θnew, |v2| |v1| sin θnew) with n = v1 × v2 and d = n × joint, where joint denotes the cartesian coordinates of the chosen joints. p1 and p2 refer to the parent joints of the chosen joints. Similarly, we rotated the skeleton vectors with the chosen joints orthogonal to the plane containing v1 and v2 by at most 0.875 radians. Through this augmentation, the model learned the angular difference in key joints. “ChannelMask” is a random mask of the x- or y-axis with a 25% probability of implementing independence of behavior contents on a specific axis. For example, if the y-axis is masked in a motion sequence fi = {xi, yi, zi}t, ChannelMask(fi) = {xi, 0, zi}t. To validate augmentation combinations through ablation analysis, we introduced existing augmentation strategies widely used in human action recognition. For the first augmentation combination20, we adopted two spatial skeleton augmentations (“Shear” and “JointJittering”) and a single temporal skeleton augmentation (“Temporal Crop-resize”). The “Shear” transformation gave variations in viewpoint and distance to the camera with pose conservation. In more detail, for the segment X ∈ Rbatchsize×numjoints×joint size, the modified action representation Shear(X) = X * [[1, r01, r02], [r10, 1, r12], [r20, r21, 1]]. “JointJittering” inserts a perturbation in joint connections through their regular movement of random joints to teach the model invariance to noise in joint positions. To achieve this, we multiplexed three randomly selected joints j, with a jitter matrix as JointJitter(X) = X[:, j, :] * [[r00, r01, r02], [r10, r11, r12], [r20, r21, r22]]. All entries in the shear and jitter matrices are randomly drawn from a uniform distribution [-1, 1]. Since “Temporal Crop-resize” adjusts a similar distortion to the “ChangeStartPoint” method, described above, we utilized our augmentation module without modification. In a second augmentation strategy, we integrated augmentation methods proposed for human depression detection48: “Shear”, “Rotate”, “GaussianNoise”, “JointMask”, and “ChannelMask”. In “Rotate”, we randomly rotated a 3D action skeleton with respect to the x-, y-, and z-axes with random variables α, β, γ ∈ Rbatchsize×1×jointsize×jointsize. “GaussianNoise” adds appropriate Gaussian noise to the action sequence. We applied the Gaussian noise matrix ε ∈ Rbatchsize×1×numjoints×jointsize, whose entries are taken from a Gaussian distribution with mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, to the action segment X ∈ Rbatchsize×inputlength×numjoints×jointsize as GaussianNoise(X) = X + ε. “JointMask” generates positive pairs by concealing three random joints by X[:, :, j, :] = 0. For self-supervised representation learning, we employed Cross-Modal Mutual Distillation (ST)49, following the structure of Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN) building encoders50. A given full-length motion sequence obtained from AVATAR studio was divided into segments with a single motion segment unit of 10, introducing a 1-frame stride to provide generalization in input action sequences. The dataset consisted of 120 label-free videos of control and depressive-like behavior model mice for 4 weeks, and each video contains a whole 36,000 frame motion sequence of freely moving mice. In the CLOSER framework, training, validation, and test datasets are generated with a ratio of 60:20:20 while randomly sorting motion sequences. We used encoders composed of 9 layers of the spatio-temporal graph convolution operators; 3 layers of 32 output channels, 3 layers of 64 output channels, and 3 layers of 128 output channels stacked in order. This implies that the encoder is designed to map the input space of R10×27 to an embedding space of R128. In the CMD modality design, we implemented two approaches, joint movement and motion change. Joint modality represents Cartesian coordinates of key points from a “fix pose” motion sequences, and motion modality defines a difference in Cartesian coordinates of key points between adjacent frames from “pose” motion sequences. For the projection head module, linear layers of input dimension I ∈ R128 and output dimension O ∈ R128 without any activation function. The model was trained to optimize InfoNCE (Info Noise-Contrastive Estimation) loss51 and Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. For InfoNCE loss LSCL and CMD loss LCMD, the total loss function L = LjointSCL + LmotionSCL + LCMD was calculated. For the size of a queue-based memory bank N and temperature hyper-parameter τ, InfoNCE loss for joint and motion modality is defined as LSCL = -log [exp(zTq zk / τ) / (exp(zTq zk / τ) + ΣNi=1 exp(zTq zmi / τ))]. The knowledge distillation was achieved by minimizing Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of similarity distributions LCMD = KL(p(zjoint, τt) || p(zmotion, τs)) + KL(p(zmotion, τt) || p(zjoint, τs)), where p(z, τ) = Σ exp(zT ni / τ) / Σ exp(zT ni / τ), i=1, 2, ..., K. All hyperparameters used to optimize the CLOSER framework are listed in Supplementary Table 3.

Temporalsegmentation.Forconsiderationoftemporaldynamicsinbehaviorsequences,wemodifiedthemajorityvotealgorithmtosplitsequentialframes into semantic motion segments.An action representation z was computed by zi = ST-GCNjoint(segmenti) for i-th segment segmenti and the projection head-free query encoder ST-GCNjoint for joint modality.In dynamic temporal segmentation, we define the set Si as Si = {segmentj | i-T+1 ≤ j ≤ i+T-1} where T is the segment length, which is set to 10. We labeled each segment in Si with k-means clustering in the embedding space, then assigned the most frequent frame-level label. Label(frame i) = argmax s∈Si Label(ST-GCNjoint(s)). The consecutive frames with identical labels were paired to represent a behavioral unit. In addition, we employed a keypoint change score function52 for further estimation of the ability of the framework to capture the robust shift in the action skeleton.

Linear regression
The linear correlation of conventional depressive-like behaviors and spontaneous behavior was driven by fitting a linear regression model given variable Xi and observations yi, the linear regression model calculates coefficients βi and residual β0 by minimization of the following equation. L = 1/2 Σ (yi - ^yi)2, where yi = β0 + βiXi. Then, we estimated the coefficient of determination, the R2 score, for the numerical expression of predictability for the dependent variable from discriminant-relevant syllables.

Anomaly detection
Model configuration. To estimate the behavioral abnormalities of the disease model mice, we employed a Message-Passing Encoder-Decoder Recurrent Neural Network (MPED-RNN) model53. At each time point t, we decomposed the 3D pose representation into a global component and a local component fi = (xi, yi, zi)t. The global component represents a motion of the body center, implying a change in the absolute position of the 3D pose representation. It is modeled as the combination of the coordinates of the body center and the body’s bounding cuboid. Hence, we defined the global components as fgt = (xg, yg, zg, w, l, h). Each feature of the global component was calculated with the following equations: xg = (max xi + min xi) / 2; yg = (max yi + min yi) / 2; zg = (max zi + min zi) / 2; w = max xi - min xi; l = max yi - min yi; h = max zi - min zi. We defined the local component as a relative motion of key joints with respect to the body center. It was calculated from the global component as follows: xl,i = (xi - xg) / w; yl,i = (yi - yg) / l; zl,i = (zi - zg) / h. We introduced encoder Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) modules and decoder GRU modules for both the global and local components to implement MPED-RNN. Each module sends messages to its counterpart and receives messages for the calculation of the latter state. The messages exchanged in the module with current state h were computed as specified below, where σ denotes the activation function, W represents the weight, and b is the bias term: messagel→g = σ(Wl→g hl + bl→g); messageg→l = σ(Wg→l hg + bg→l). Then, to generate training segments, we used a utilized sliding-window strategy as follows: segment i = {ft} t=bi::ei for bi = s×i, ei = s×i+T, where the sliding stride s=10 and the segment length T=60. In model training, we measured reconstruction and prediction loss using the loss function suggested by Morais, Romero, et al.: L = 1/T Σ ||f*t - f*t||2 + 1/P Σ ||f*t - f*t||2, where P represents prediction length, which was set to 30, and * denotes either l or g. The training and validation datasets were split into an 80:20 ratio. To calculate the frame anomaly score, we used the following equation: anomaly score(frame i) = Σ segment∈Si fT l,gL * (segment), where Si = {segmentj | i-T+1 ≤ j ≤ i+T-1} denotes the set of segments containing frame i. For simplicity, we only considered frames belonging to T segments and analyzed the distribution of frame-wise anomaly scores for the evaluation of abnormality in the disease group compared to its control group.

Visualization. To visualize the embedding spaces of the global and local components, we leveraged an unsupervised deep anomaly detection approach called LatentOut, which was developed by Fabrizio Angiulli et al.29. With the mean μ and standard deviation for an anomaly score distribution σ, we normalized anomaly scores with the following equation: anomaly normalized score(frame i) = (anomaly score(frame i) - μ) / σ. Then, we projected the results for the embedding structure of global and local components using PCA onto a 3D coordinate system with the z-axis defined as z(frame i) = Σ frame∈Nk (frame i) anomaly score normalized(frame), where Nk(:) is the k-nearest-neighbor using default parameters (k=5). In the k-nearest neighbor module, distance was defined as Euclidean distance between projected cartesian coordinates and the normalized anomaly score.

Hierarchical clustering
To estimate the overall clustering structure of the CLOSER framework, we performed a hierarchical recategorization of the embedding. An average embedding zc for behavioral cluster c was measured according to zc = Σ zi / N, where zi is the embedding information of the ith segment in cluster c, and N is the number of segments in cluster c. We leveraged the Scikit-learn (sklearn) module for agglomerative clustering to group clustered objects based on similarity using complete linkage.

Dimensionality reduction
Principal component analysis (PCA). To extract the features of high-dimensional behavioral sequences using variance-maximizing projection54, we employed the Scikit-learn implementation of PCA with 13 components, with default parameters: (i) whiten=False, which determines the original variance in scalar values, (ii) svd solver=0auto0, which solves based on the input dimensions and the chosen number of components.

Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP). We introduced UMAP to perform nonlinear dimensionality reduction, with the preservation of the topological structure of behavioral data within a low-dimensional embedding55. We leveraged the UMAP implementation in 13-dimension, with default settings: (i) n neighbors=15, (ii) min dist=0.1, and (iii) metric=0euclidean0 in pairwise distance measurements.

Benchmarking
To estimate the quality of the embedding precisely, we compared it to that of existing motion analysis frameworks, VAME and keypoint-MoSeq. Variational animal motion embedding (VAME). For the VAME, we modified the input structure to accept 3D behavioral segments as input through the extension of the number of features, from 12 to 27, and the embedding dimension, from 30-dimension to 108-dimension. In model training and inference, we adjusted the frame lengths of reconstruction and prediction methods to ten and five frames, respectively. All 3D pose trajectories were concatenated across animals and conditions and then windowed into 10-frame segments. Each segment was normalized and fed into the VAME encoder in batches of 4096 segments. From each batch, the VAME encoder produced a 4096×108 array of latent means (μ), followed by the concatenation of all batches to reconstruct a full embedding matrix. As the variational autoencoder architecture of the VAME consists of an encoder and a decoder, each using GRUs, we trained the model with the given parameters for reconstruction, prediction, and KL divergence, which shows the maximal performance in behavioral classification. For the i-th segment segment, we generated the action representation zi = VAMEencoder(segmenti). We applied both a Hidden Markov Model and k-means clustering after majority voting to assign frame-wise cluster labels.

Keypoint-MoSeq. For the keypoint-MoSeq, we configured the model to align with its key joints and connections, maintaining consistency with the variational autoencoder structure. The 3D pose trajectories were loaded and directly subjected to PCA, while omitting the noise-calibration step, which had been applied in AVATAR calibration. We then initialized and fit an autoregressive hidden Markov model on the PCA projections, followed by fitting the MoSeq model. Calculated inferred state sequences were exported to obtain frame-wise behavioral syllable labels for downstream analysis.

Investigation of representative behavior phenotypes
A behavior segmentation system requires the ability to cluster motion sequences into discrete modules of action for further ethological interpretation. Hence, we inspected exemplary behavior phenotypes (i.e., walking, turning, rearing, and falling) from automatically categorized motion segments to identify the semantic implementation of the framework. For behavior segments longer than 10 frames, we equally divided the segments into 10 sections and averaged each metric over a single section to summarize the behavioral features on an identical time scale. The set of frames Fn involved in cluster n was defined as Fn = {Fi = (xi, yi, zi) | j ∈ Joint, s ≤ i ≤ e} with start frame s and end frame e for key joints Joint. The i-th behavior segment in “walking” clusters was evaluated with moving distance d where dist(:,:) denotes the Euclidean distance between two body points from consecutive time sections t and t-1. di = 1/N Σ dist(xj, yj, zj, xj-1, yj-1, zj-1), N = e-s+1, s+(i-1)N+1 ≤ t ≤ s+iN. To measure the degree of “turning”, we measured the angle ai = 1/N Σ angle(v1, v2), N = e-s+1, s+(i-1)N+1 ≤ t ≤ s+iN between the anus-body center vector, v1, and the body center head vector, v2, where angle(v1, v2) = acos(v1·v2 / |v1||v2|). For the qualification of behavior segments in “rearing” and “falling”, we measured the height of the nose as follows: hi = 1/N Σ znose,t, N = e-s+1, s+(i-1)N+1 ≤ t ≤ s+iN.

Normalization
We normalized the frequency and transition probabilities for the behavioral clusters using the initial behavior structure while considering individual variance in the exploratory behavior paradigm throughout the subjects. We implemented fold change of a cluster frequency Freq and transition probability p for the k-th segment xk: FreqNorm(c, week, mouse) = Σ j f(xk | xk ∈ week m ∩ mouse n, Label(xk) = c) / Σ l m n j f(xk | xk ∈ week m ∩ mouse n, Label(xk) = c), pNorm(ci → cj, week, mouse) = Σ k f(xk-1, xk | xk-1, xk ∈ week m ∩ mouse n, Label(xk-1) = ci, Label(xk) = cj) / Σ k f(xk-1, xk | xk-1, xk ∈ week m ∩ mouse n, Label(xk-1) = ci, Label(xk) = cj).

Linear discriminant analysis (LDA)
To calculate the class-separability through a dimensionality reduction, we projected the training configuration of Linear Discriminant Analysis (in sklearn) results into the plane (nx, ny)projected = LDA(ST-GCNjoint(xi)) for labeled data x = {t, t, y=c}.

Pearson correlation coefficient
We calculated the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) by dividing the covariance of the variables by the product of their standard deviations, yielding a value between -1 and 1, as follows: rxy = E[(X-μX)(Y-μY)] / σX σY, where X and Y are latent vectors, μX and μY are respective means, and σX and σY are standard deviations.

k-nearest neighbor classifier
For quality evaluation of latent embedding, we employed a non-parametric, k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) classifier that predicts the label of an input instance by identification of the k closest labeled neighbors within the feature space and assignment of label using majority voting. We utilized the KNeighborsClassifier from the Scikit-learn library with default parameters: five neighbors (Nneighbors = 5) with uniform voting weights, using the Minkowski distance (p=2) corresponding to the Euclidean metric. The classifier was configured to automatically select an optimal search algorithm (algorithm=0auto0) with a leaf size of 30, without additional metric parameters.

Random forest classifier
To verify the behavioral correlation between free movement and depressive-like behaviors, we obtained the confusion matrix for control and depressive-like behavior model mice utilizing the Random Forest Classifier (from sklearn) with default settings. The Random Forest Classifier was trained with five-fold validation. To prepare the dataset, we partitioned 20-min sample recording videos into 5-min sections and calculated fold changes for cluster frequencies and transition probabilities as described in “Normalization”. To validate the size invariance of CLOSER and other benchmarking algorithms, eighty male and female mice were divided into five weight categories, spanning 18 g to 28 g in 2-g increments. The Random Forest classifier was trained to predict the weight categories from the embedding vectors extracted in non-overlapping 100-frame strides from behavioral sequences. We trained the classifier with 5-fold cross-validation in the default setting and evaluated the performance using precision, recall, and F1 score.

SHapley additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis
To investigate the influence of behavioral cluster frequencies on classifier decisions, we applied a SHAP analysis56 using the scikit-learn library. Initially, we trained a Random Forest Classifier without employing k-fold validation followed by TreeSHAP57, which defines the value function through conditional expectation to extract SHAP values. Given the feature set N, a subset S, the classifier function f, and the input x, fS(x) denotes the classifier output restricted to S, which can be further described as the conditional expectation fS(x) = E[f(x) | xS]. The SHAP value for the i-th feature was then calculated as follows: ϕi = Σ S⊆N\{i} |S|!(|N|-|S|-1)! / |N|! [fS∪{i}(x) - fS(x)]. Leveraging the additivity of the SHAP value, average absolute SHAP values for overall feature importance were calculated and depicted as cumulative bar graphs, while SHAP values for individual groups were represented using beeswarm plots.

Transition probability
The transition probability from behavioral cluster ci to behavioral cluster cj = w was calculated from the transition rate from the behavioral cluster of the k-th segment xk: pi→j = Σ k f(xk-1, xk | Label(xk-1) = ci, Label(xk) = cj) / Σ k f(xk-1 | Label(xk-1) = ci). To compute the change in transition probability for a behavioral cluster, we estimated the difference of each transition probability and visualized leveraging the network analysis framework NetworkX. Only transitions whose alteration was significant (p<0.05) were displayed in transition graphs.

Statistics
Statistical analysis and graphs were produced in Python (3.10.12) and GraphPad Prism 10. Time-series datasets were analyzed by two-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse corrections. Post hoc analysis for multiple comparisons leveraged the Benjamini–Hochberg test to control the false discovery rate, which we fixed at 0.05. For the estimation of significance in groups of more than two, we estimated one-way ANOVAs with a 95% confidence interval and Dunnett’s post hoc analysis for multiple comparisons to the control group. Two-group comparisons, including those for syllable usage and syllable subset analysis, were performed using two-tailed unpaired t-tests (parametric) if the group passed the Anderson–Darling (AD) normality test. Otherwise, we used a Mann–Whitney test (non-parametric) to deal with a non-Gaussian distribution. Classification performance of k-NN and random forest classifiers was summarized with average values and standard deviation of precision, recall, and F1 scores. Box graphs show the 25th–75th percentiles for the whole dataset with a line indicating the median. Bar graphs and timelines present means ± standard error of the mean. Asterisks denote levels of statistical significance as follows: *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001, and ****p<0.001. More detailed descriptions are summarized in Supplementary Data 1, with statistical significance marked with yellow blocks.

### Reviewer 2

Here, Oh and colleagues describe a self-supervised approach for segmenting three-dimensional keypoint trajectories into discrete behaviors that they call CLOSER. Specifically, CLOSER leverages self-supervised learning – a technique increasingly being used for action segmentation in human data – to learn an embedding of 3D kinematic data from spontaneously behaving mice. The learning objective is constructed to learn an embedding space where points representing similar behaviors are close together and dissimilar behaviors are far apart, while also remaining invariant to “nuisance” features such as body size. Points in the embedding space are clustered to form a segmentation of 3D kinematic data into discrete behaviors. They benchmark CLOSER against the currents state-of-the-art, Keypoint-MoSeq (KP-MoSeq) and Variational Animal Motion Embedding (VAME), and find that their technique has better correspondence with manual labels. Major problems that must be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication:

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript presents CLOSER, a self-supervised contrastive learning framework designed to analyze spontaneous rodent behavior in a chronic mild stress model of depression. This approach represents a step forward in behavior quantification by integrating 3D skeleton tracking and unsupervised learning. CLOSER provides a tool for advancing preclinical psychiatric research, particularly in identifying nuanced depressive-like behaviors and tracking responses to antidepressant treatments in a more ecologically valid setting.
Key contributions of the manuscript include the following:
First, CLOSER enhances behavior quantification by integrating 3D pose skeleton data, which captures detailed motion patterns and adds granularity to behavioral segmentation. This approach enables a more refined quantification of behavior, which is especially beneficial for nuanced analyses in psychiatric and behavioral neuroscience research.
Second, the framework leverages a self-supervised contrastive learning approach, organizing behavioral representations effectively without reliance on labeled data. While contrastive lost is common in other areas of ML it was not applied to animal behavior quantification yet.
Third, CLOSER applies its analytical power to the Chronic Mild Stress (CUMS) model, identifying behavior changes associated with chronic stress in rodents and revealing sex-specific and time-dependent behavior patterns. These findings offer insights into the differential impact of chronic stress on behavior, and the model’s application to pharmacological studies demonstrates its potential for preclinical drug screening.
Finally, the model shows potential for creating standardized, reproducible behavioral assays, with the ability to quantify behavioral changes linked to both depressive-like phenotypes and antidepressant responses. This represents a promising advancement for translational research and reproducibility in animal models of psychiatric disorders.
CLOSER’s implementation builds upon the MoCo (Momentum Contrast) framework by Meta, incorporating several similar components for contrastive learning, such as a dual encoder system, momentum-based updates, and a projection head. The model architecture mirrors MoCo’s query-key structure, with two encoders to process different behavioral data modalities, stabilized by a momentum mechanism that supports consistent embeddings over time.
The originality in CLOSER lies in its domain-specific adaptations, such as using 3D skeletal and kinematic data and tailoring augmentations to the behavioral nuances of rodents. However, the modifications are incremental rather than fundamentally new: they focus on adapting MoCo’s principles to the nuances of behavior analysis rather than introducing novel learning techniques or architectural elements.
Despite these contributions, there are several points that raise questions and could benefit from further clarification or refinement.
Major points:
First, while the reported accuracy increase over VAME is an improvement, it remains marginal. The absence of error bars or confidence intervals for the reported benchmarks raises questions about the robustness and generalizability of these findings, especially considering potential dataset-specific effects or stochastic variations. Including error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests would support the accuracy claims and enhance clarity regarding model generalizability across different datasets.
Second, the use of 3D skeleton data indeed enhances behavioral segmentation, yet this could likely be achieved by combining DANNCE or similar 3D tracking tools with VAME. This integration raises questions regarding the necessity of developing an entirely new model to incorporate 3D capabilities. Comparing CLOSER’s performance with a 3D-augmented VAME (i.e. running DANNCE and adding the 3D data as input to VAME) would clarify whether CLOSER’s use of contrastive learning advantages over an adaptation of existing frameworks, or if the improvement stems only by the fact that more data (3D coordinates) are fed to the model.
Third, while the findings on chronic stress-induced behavior changes are compelling, it remains unclear if these insights are due to the unique capabilities of CLOSER or simply the result of analyzing a new benchmark model. Including baseline results with existing models for the same chronic stress data would help establish the unique value of CLOSER’s findings in this context.
Finally, the paper does not provide a detailed comparison of the findings related to the CUMS model with existing literature to establish their novelty in the neuroscience field. Without such a comparison, it's challenging to determine whether these behavioral patterns represent new discoveries in neuroscience or if they align with previously reported observations. Have there been perhaps some new substantial findings using the new method that have been not known so far?
In terms of reproducibility, while the code is available, the absence of example datasets limits the ability of other researchers to replicate the findings or to test the model on new datasets. Providing a sample dataset or detailed data specifications would allow others to reproduce the results for reviewers AND readers and evaluate CLOSER’s effectiveness across diverse datasets.
Minor points:
The manuscript presents confusion matrices for classifier accuracy, but the interpretation of these matrices is limited without details on error patterns. This limitation restricts insights into potential misclassifications. Adding evaluation metrics like precision, recall, and F1 scores, along with error bars, could illustrate model reliability and provide a more comprehensive understanding of classification performance.
The use of LDA to visualize antidepressant effectiveness could be strengthened by a rationale for its selection over other dimensionality reduction techniques. Including a comparison with alternatives like t-SNE or UMAP would offer a broader perspective on clustering patterns and lend further support to the use of LDA.
The robustness and interpretability of SHAP summary plots for antidepressant efficacy would benefit from both global and individual feature importance, helping to identify consistent features across different conditions. Presenting individual SHAP values for specific animals or conditions could clarify which features are universally important or context-dependent in the assessment of antidepressant efficacy.
The interpretability of the results for drug classifications based on confusion matrices is unclear. Supplementing these matrices with precision-recall metrics or analyzing specific types of errors (e.g., false positives vs. false negatives) could offer insights into the model’s strengths and weaknesses in classifying stress conditions and drug responses. Clarifying why certain drugs or conditions are more challenging to classify would make the results more actionable.
The syllable usage and transition analyses would benefit from statistical validation to support claims of generalizability. Adding statistical tests, such as permutation tests, and validating the results on additional datasets would reinforce the claims of generalizability.
The reliance on balanced accuracy as the sole metric for classifier accuracy may not fully capture the model’s performance in distinguishing depressive symptoms. Including metrics like sensitivity and specificity would offer a comprehensive evaluation and ensure that the classifier’s performance reflects accuracy across various symptom categories.

Final Verdict
While CLOSER is a carefully implemented application of contrastive learning for analyzing rodent behavior, its contributions appear primarily incremental. The model heavily relies on the established MoCo framework, with adaptations that are domain-specific but do not introduce fundamentally new methodologies or architectural innovations. These modifications—such as using 3D skeletal data and behavior-specific augmentations—tailor MoCo’s principles to the nuances of rodent behavior analysis but lack technical novelty.
Furthermore, the manuscript does not clearly establish whether its primary contribution lies in the methodological adaptation or in producing new insights within the neuroscience of depressive behavior. Although it reports findings of sex-specific and time-dependent behavior changes in a chronic stress model, the novelty of these results for neuroscience is not convincingly discussed (hopefully this will be confirmed with reviewers with more understanding of the particular field). Without detailed comparisons with existing literature, it is challenging to assess whether these behavioral observations offer new understanding or align with previously known patterns.
For these reasons, the paper would benefit from a clearer positioning of its main contribution—whether as a novel behavioral quantification tool or a source of new biological insights—and from substantial additional justification for the technical and scientific novelty of its findings. The the authors should aim to clearly establish unique methodological contributions that distinguish CLOSER from existing models like MoCo, provide detailed comparative benchmarks to demonstrate added value over simple adaptations of MoCo, and strengthen generalizability through robust statistical validation.

Response: We appreciate the reviewer for the critical feedback and hope to have addressed all the reviewer’s concerns in our responses below.
Comment 1. The authors are correct to, in the Introduction, be highly critical of the readout tests of the forced swim test and tail suspension test, given their lack of face validity. However, they then proceed to use these very same tests to compare the behavioral effects of chronic stress in standardized tests with that in their locomotion paradigm. Furthermore, they interpret the effects of stress in the standardized tests in a highly subjective way of mice really being in a state of "despair" or "helplessness". These are antidepressant screening tests and do not provide information relevant to the major symptoms of depression. Examples of translational behavioral paradigms relevant to major depression symptoms would be reward motivation and Pavlovian fear conditioning.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important issue about the interpretation of conventional behavioral tests (FST, TST, and SPT), and fully agree that these tests have significant limitations in construct validity, yet they remain essential for validation of the depression models in mice. Although our manuscript primarily aims to demonstrate the utility of motion profiles from naturalistic behavior analysis for depression diagnosis, initial validation of depression models using these conventional tests was a necessary foundational step.
However, we acknowledge that our earlier descriptions might have overly linked the conventional behavioral tests to our behavioral analysis, potentially undermining the novelty and application of our new methodological framework. Thus, we have revised our manuscript to remove excessive comparisons between conventional antidepressant screening tests and naturalistic behavior patterns in our new analysis of monoaminergic and non-monoaminergic antidepressants (Figure 5). The current manuscript describes antidepressant efficacy measured through conventional tests more cautiously as follows (Results, line 402):
“[…] We administered traditional monoaminergic antidepressants (fluoxetine and imipramine) or emerging non-monoaminergic candidates (agmatine, scopolamine, and rapastinel) to observe the distinct action of different drug groups. In chronically stressed male mice, most antidepressants significantly reduced immobility durations in FST, while imipramine alone enhanced sucrose preference rather than influencing immobility (Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). Additionally, rapastinel treatment significantly elevated sucrose preference, whereas other drugs did not induce significant improvements in either the TST or SPT. Thus, despite the high predictive validity of FST in male mice, traditional behavioral assays generally failed to differentiate individual or grouped antidepressant actions, with the exception of imipramine and rapastinel.”
Moreover, while FST and TST are widely used to represent behavioral despair1, we agree that these tests alone could not capture learned helplessness. Thus, we have removed the term ‘learned helplessness’ from our manuscript and replaced any use of the phrase ‘depressive symptom’ with the more precise term ‘depressive-like behavior’ or ‘depressive-like phenotypes’ to avoid overstating the clinical implications of our findings:
 Line 193: “In male CUS mice, we observed a significant increase in behavioral despair (TST, FST) (Fig. 3a, b, left) and anhedonia (SPT) (Fig. 3c, left), as well as a decrease in body weight (Fig. 3d).”
 Line 262: “In addition, syllable frequency was more closely related to depressive-like behaviors reflecting behavioral despair (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b, d, and e) than anhedonia (Supplementary Fig. 6c, f) in both males and females, as an analogous result has been observed in the previous study utilizing social defeat stress mice for depressive disorder model.”
 Line 361: “These results with conventional assays were sufficient to confirm the expression of depressive-like behaviors, but they failed to show a direct correlation with specific time points in the CUS paradigm.”
Comment 2. The manner in which the authors describe the outputs of their algorithm renders it impossible to comprehend what actual behavioral changes they observed in locomotion in a semi-naturalistic environment and how this might be relevant to major symptoms of depression. In principle, it would be very interesting to know what locomotor changes are induced by chronic stress, but the data needs to be presented in a way that is understandable and uses measures of overall activity, general body posture, etc.
Response:
We fully agree with the reviewer that a comprehensive analysis of kinematics for syllables altered by chronic stress could provide potential readers a clear interpretation of behavioral characteristics. To address the concern, we performed a time-series kinematic analysis of depression-related syllables by measuring four motion metrics: nose height, body angle, body shift, and nose shift. We then grouped syllables that significantly increased or decreased following chronic stress and extracted representative 3D action skeleton sequences to visualize body posture and dynamics. We incorporated the analysis result in the new Supplementary Figure 5.

In male mice, we observed a reduction in motifs with elevated body angles and sniff-related motifs, which show larger nose shifts than body shifts. Conversely, syllables that increased under stress featured higher nose heights. In females, stress-elevated syllables showed comparatively greater body angles, corresponding to turning behaviors in manual annotations. These findings are now described in the manuscript (Results, line 249).
“[…] In further kinematic profiling, chronic stress selectively reduced the occurrence of motifs with elevated body angles and sniff-related behaviors with large nose shifts relative to body shifts (Supplementary Fig. 5a), while higher nose heights were observed in stress-elevated syllables (Supplementary Fig. 5b). In female mice, stress-elevated syllables displayed greater body angles, in agreement with manual annotation, turning behaviors.”
Reviewer #2
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Here, Oh and colleagues describe a self-supervised approach for segmenting three-dimensional keypoint trajectories into discrete behaviors that they call CLOSER. Specifically, CLOSER leverages self-supervised learning – a technique increasingly being used for action segmentation in human data – to learn an embedding of 3D kinematic data from spontaneously behaving mice. The learning objective is constructed to learn an embedding space where points representing similar behaviors are close together and dissimilar behaviors are far apart, while also remaining invariant to “nuisance” features such as body size. Points in the embedding space are clustered to form a segmentation of 3D kinematic data into discrete behaviors. They benchmark CLOSER against the currents state-of-the-art, Keypoint-MoSeq (KP-MoSeq) and Variational Animal Motion Embedding (VAME), and find that their technique has better correspondence with manual labels. Finally, the authors demonstrate that CLOSER can be used to dissect the behavioral consequences of inducing depression in a chronic stress model.
Overall, I found that the authors have an intriguing idea that is likely to be well-received by the Nature Communications readership. However, I found some major technical issues that must be addressed before this can be considered for publication. I hope most of this can be remedied by some analytic controls without any additional experiments.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer for their helpful and constructive comments. Please see below for our detailed responses.
Major problems that must be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication:
Major comments:
Comment 1. Contrastive learning is used to learn an embedding space of 3D kinematic data that is purportedly sensitive to changes in behavior and insensitive to other factors such as mouse size. This is a reasonable approach in principle; however, unless I missed it, I found no validation that their method achieves the stated objective.
Response:
The reviewer raises a relevant point that was not fully clear in the previous manuscript. We agree with the reviewer that the characterization of invariances in our module is mandatory to fully validate the contrastive learning training process. In this regard, we performed additional computational analysis and addressed all comments in detail below.
Comment 1a. Specifically, the authors do not provide evidence that CLOSER’s embedding strategy is actually invariant to size while remaining sensitive to the differences between kinematically distinct behaviors. Here, the authors need to provide direct quantification that their embedding space, as they say, works better than PCA, autoencoders, t-SNE, etc (line 380). This cannot be asserted without direct quantification. A simple path would be to use their manual labels and quantify the average distance between all pairs of points in different manually identified behavioral states and within behavioral states but across different subjects, especially across subjects with different weights and sizes.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments on the evaluation of the embedding structure. In addition to the extrinsic evaluation presented earlier, we performed a comprehensive intrinsic analysis to estimate the quality of the embedding space. We employed the Pearson correlation coefficient to quantitatively assess intra- and inter-cluster correlations across multiple embedding methods, including CLOSER, VAME, and other pose representations (PCA and UMAP).
To investigate the invariance to factors, in our case, mouse size, individuality, and sex, we calculated the correlation coefficients across distinct mouse subjects and sexes. The underlying rationale was that if a variable is learned as invariant, the intra-cluster correlations from different animals should be significantly higher than the inter-cluster correlations. Indeed, our analysis revealed that CLOSER achieves high intra-cluster correlation and low inter-cluster correlation for these variables, confirming that it captures behavioral features independent of size, sex, and individuality. A similar analysis of VAME demonstrated a clear separation of correlations, whereas the 3D pose representation (including PCA and UMAP) showed minimal difference or opposite trend, indicating poorer cluster distinction. These additional results are now included in the Results section (line 157) of the revised manuscript and the new Supplementary Figure 2.
“[…] For further intrinsic evaluation of embedding spaces, we calculated the Pearson correlation, which quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two behavioral segments. Using this method, we evaluated whether our augmentation strategy induced invariance within the embedding space, such that syllable definitions depended solely on motion sequences. To achieve this, we selected two distinct syllables from mice differing in weight, individuality, or sex, and computed the intra- and inter-cluster correlation coefficients (Supplementary Fig. 2). In analysis, CLOSER exhibited high intra-cluster correlations alongside minimal inter-cluster correlations across all tested conditions, implying that the latent structure is independent to these three variables. Likewise, VAME showed strong intra-cluster correlation and negative inter-cluster correlations, whereas embeddings derived directly from 3D pose representations (including PCA and UMAP) displayed low intra-cluster correlation or greater variance, reflecting poor cluster separation.”
Furthermore, to evaluate the reproducibility of our embeddings on unseen human-labeled data, we compared intra- and inter-cluster correlations across two independent mouse labeling datasets. Consistently, we observed higher intra-cluster correlations across most of the clusters (except for cluster 2, right turn, and cluster 5, freezing with four paws), which emphasizes that CLOSER effectively learns invariant and discriminative behavioral features.
Comment 1b. Second, it would be extremely useful to show that, if their embedding shows better qualities than alternatives, how important the specifics of their augmentation strategy are. The authors use the prediction accuracy of manually identified labels to validate their particular combination of augmentations. This should be complemented by analyzing the geometry of their embedding (see point above) and repeating this analysis across different combinations of augmentation functions.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestion on an estimation of the augmentation strategies. While we have listed the accuracies of behavioral prediction for augmentation combinations, we have now incorporated the geometric analysis of embedding space into a revised manuscript to address this point more clearly. In detail, we extended our intrinsic evaluation across multiple augmentation combinations using an unseen human-labeled dataset with 13 manually defined clusters to strengthen the following points:
1) Impact of augmentations on embedding geometry: For each augmentation combination, we computed intra- and inter-cluster Pearson correlations. The selected augmentation strategy produced the highest gap between intra- and inter-cluster correlation (Supplementary Figure 1). Compared to other moderate augmentation methods, our combination enhanced the embedding quality of grooming behaviors.
2) Correlation between geometry and task performance: We observed a relationship that augmentation schemes with high clustering consistency also showed high classification metrics.
3) Justification of the augmentation strategy through additional performance validation: We measured precision, recall, and F1 scores on the human-labeled test set and proved that our augmentation strategy consistently outperformed other augmentations (Supplementary Table 1).
These new analyses confirm that our mouse-specific augmentation combination is critical for learning invariant, discriminative behavioral embeddings. We have now addressed this point in the Results section (line 117) as follows:
“Next, to evaluate the geometric variance of latent spaces across multiple augmentation strategies, we measured Pearson correlation coefficients for representations of 13 manually labeled behaviors (Supplementary Table 2) in an unseen human dataset to compare within- (or intra-) and between (or inter)-cluster relationships. A coefficient of +1 or -1 denotes perfect positive or negative linear association, respectively, while 0 indicates no linear relationship. We found that augmentation schemes with superior classification accuracy also exhibited stronger intra-cluster correlation than inter-cluster correlation. Importantly, the mouse-optimized augmentation yielded enhanced embedding for grooming behaviors (clusters 6 and 7) compared with augmentation combinations lacking channel masking (strategy 3) or scaling (strategy 2), highlighting the necessity of a complete augmentation strategy for mouse behavior latent structures.”
Comment 1c. Third, I was a little puzzled by some of the augmentations. If I understand correctly, Scale simply scales x, y, and z coordinates by the same factor. Can the authors justify why this is a reasonable thing to do? Can keypoint coordinates across different mouse sizes truly be reduced to a single scaling factor across x, y, and z?
Response:
The reviewer raised an important point about scaling augmentation in contrastive learning. We understand that the multiplication of a single scaling factor on 3D keypoint coordinates seems unelaborated and inadequate for the augmentation method. First of all, scaling and resize augmentation is a well-known augmentation method for enforcing size invariance in contrastive learning, and these methods have been employed in the action recognition field (Fida Mohammad Thoker et al., 2021) (Jingjing Yang et al., 2022) (Jiahang Zhang et al., 2023).
Notably, as a contrastive learning framework learns an invariance between two augmented views from the same data, the model learns that action skeletons with different scaling factors represent the same behavior by minimizing the distances between augmented views in the feature space. Truly, it is a nature of contrastive learning that the encoder of the model is invariant to linear scaling of the mouse size, as stated in Ting Chen et al. (2020) and Kaiming He et al. (2020).
However, as the reviewer pointed out, there should be additional validation for whether scaling 3D coordinates by the same factor reduces or enlarges the size of a mouse maintaining pose information. To clarify this confusion, we extracted a random segment and visualized it in 3D space after applying ‘Scale’, ‘ChangeAngle’, and ‘ChangeStartPoint’ augmentations. The original and scaled 3D action skeletons implied that multiplying a single scaling factor is sufficient for size scaling without pose distortion.
Comment 2. The performance comparison with VAME and KP-MoSeq, which is central to the manuscript, is confusing.
Comment 2a. If I understand correctly, the authors specifically tailored their augmentation strategy (Sup. Table 1) to maximize prediction accuracy on the same dataset that is used for the performance comparison in Figure 2. If this is the case, then the authors need to come up with two completely separate datasets – one for tuning hyperparameters and another for performance evaluation. Either way, any hyperparameters in VAME and KP-MoSeq must also be tuned in the same fashion; that is, if the authors are going to tune hyperparameters of their own algorithm to maximize performance, then this must be done with all other algorithms to foster a fair comparison.
Response:
We fully agree with the reviewer that the performance comparison for the CLOSER, VAME, and KP-MoSeq should be analyzed in various hyperparameter conditions to evaluate the maximal performance of other methods. Therefore, in the revision process, we carefully examined the model performance by adjusting four parts of the measurement of behavior prediction accuracy: 1) employment of the embedding distance-based classifier, 2) introduction of an independent test dataset, 3) subtle hyperparameter tuning in VAME, and 4) specification of hyperparameters in CLOSER.
In detail:
1) We discarded an action module using a simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP) decoder. Commonly, self-supervised learning is operated in pre-training models using encoder architectures, then fine-tuned for specific downstream tasks after the addition of decoders. Accordingly, we adopted an exemplary algorithm in the BERT framework to investigate whether the amount and quality of information in embeddings are sufficient to be decoded into action modules using a simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP), and trained a two-layer MLP with a hidden dimension size of 100 and a RELU activation function for action module prediction. However, we found that the structure of the embedding space cannot be accurately estimated in the presence of a decoder if K-means clustering or Hidden Markov Model (HMM) are performed directly on the embedding structure. Fortunately, the k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) probing exhibits a high efficiency without any distribution assumption and is a reliable indicator of downstream task performance2. Indeed, many studies have employed the k-NN classifier to assess the quality of the latent space3,4. Hence, we revised our validation, adopting the k-NN classifier in embedding space qualification throughout the study.
2) To ensure the fairness of the comparison step, we generated an independent test dataset that was never seen during the training process. Similar to the original data production, we assigned one of thirteen behavior labels in Supplementary Table 2 to each video frame for a freely moving mouse.
3) Regarding the hyperparameter tuning in the VAME framework, we listed the default and optimized hyperparameters of VAME in the table below. It must be highlighted that we modified the VAME structure to develop an optimal environment comparable to our framework. The VAME structure, which originally managed 2D skeletal input, was adjusted to receive a 3D action skeleton while complying with the ratio of hidden dimension. Also, we reshaped the 30-frame reconstruction / 15-frame prediction training format into a 10-frame reconstruction / 5-frame prediction to compare with other methods without bias. In addition to former optimizations, we further modulated the learning rate and the number of maximum epochs in the revised manuscript, allowing us to monitor the effect of hyperparameter manipulation. The classification performance of VAME trained with two learning rates (5e-4 or 1e-3) and two maximum epochs (500 or 20) was tested.

“Variational Animal Motion Embedding (VAME). For the VAME, we modified the input structure to accept 3D behavioral segments as input through the extension of the number of features, from 12 to 27, and the embedding dimension, from 30-dimension to 108-dimension. In model training and inference, we adjusted the frame lengths of reconstruction and prediction methods to ten and five frames, respectively. Along with the modification of the benchmarking embedding of Keypoint-MoSeq as described in Comment 2b, we re-analyzed the performance of the behavioral classification across different methods. As a result, our framework exhibited the highest balanced (66%) and top-1 (55%) accuracy. Moreover, additional metrics revealed that CLOSER consistently showed strong precision, recall, and F1 scores. Comment 2b. Can the authors elaborate on the embedding space that was used for KP-MoSeq? KP-MoSeq is not really an embedding algorithm, it simply uses PCA of keypoint trajectories as the input space for a probabilistic time series model. Did the authors attempt to make predictions using an MLP using the standard input for KP-MoSeq? If so, the authors need to make it clear that they’re not comparing their algorithm to KP-MoSeq, but rather to the input of KP-MoSeq. If I am misunderstanding what they did, and they in fact used the output of the model, how were the model hyperparameters tuned?
Response:
The reviewer raises a valid concern that keypoint-MoSeq uses the PCA projection of keypoint trajectories only as an input for its sequential analysis. Indeed, keypoint-MoSeq employs an HMM that learns transition probabilities between states, behavioral syllables IDs, and emission probabilities from a given PCA projection of motion sequences. In the previous analysis, we employed linear evaluation to assess the quality of behavior representations, excluding the segmentation step. Based on this framework, we initially believed that it was reasonable to use the 13-dimensional PCA projection of individual frames (i.e., the input to the HMM) as the behavior representation of keypoint-MoSeq in performance estimation. To account for sequential context, we concatenated 10 consecutive frames of these PCA projections to create 10-frame-length behavioral segments. However, we recognize that evaluating the input of keypoint-MoSeq alone does not fully capture the motion recognition efficiency of the entire tool. To address this limitation, we now provide an alternative comparison utilizing dimensionality reduction methods (PCA and UMAP) on raw data, comprising 270-dimensional vectors representing the 3D coordinates of keypoints over 10 consecutive frames, instead of the keypoint-MoSeq input. We have included the result of the performance comparison with raw pose data (270 dimensions), PCA (13 dimensions, identical to Keypoint-MoSeq input dimension), and UMAP (13 dimensions), and addressed the detailed description, in conjunction with our response to Comment 2b. Moreover, we have revised the Results section (line 150) to clarify the employment of the PCA and UMAP embedding as follows:
“[…] Since keypoint-MoSeq employs an HMM that learns transition probabilities between states, behavioral syllables IDs, and emission probabilities from a given 13-dimensional Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projection of motion sequences, we leveraged 270-dimension representation with 13-dimension PCA and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) embedding for 10-frame length behavioral segments, instead of keypoint-MoSeq. […]”
Comment 2c. The comparison with VAME seems more apples to apples than the comparison with KP-MoSeq, which is good. That said, the performance difference between the two algorithms looks fairly subtle (Fig. 2c), and as mentioned above, the hyperparameters of CLOSER appear to have been tuned for maximum performance. Were the hyperparameters of VAME tuned at all? If not, this must be done in the same way hyperparameters were tuned for CLOSER. Additionally, given that the performance difference between CLOSER and VAME is small, the authors should provide uncertainty estimates using different cross-validation folds or multiple restarts of each model with different random seeds.
Response:
We believe that, to some extent, the answers concerning comment 2a are applicable to this note. As previously discussed in the response, the performance of VAME in manual labeling prediction was calculated by a effective k-NN evaluation method in various hyperparameter conditions, which allows subtle tuning of the VAME framework in our environment. This analysis revealed that the classification performance of VAME was the highest with the original hyperparameter combinations. Notably, the CLOSER framework outperformed the VAME and other dimensionality reduction algorithms (e.g., PCA and UMAP), highlighting that the feature space of CLOSER is well fitted to human labeling consensus. We also incorporated statistics for the 5-fold cross-validation process under the classification performance matrices (Figure 2c) to clarify the performance estimation step.
Comment 3. Another relevant detail here is that AVATAR uses a different form of keypoint tracking. Rather than using a standard markerless keypoint tracker, my understanding is that AVATAR learns the centroid of pixels associated with a given body part. If so, can the authors elaborate on the noise characteristics of this type of tracking relative to the output of, e.g., DeepLabCut, SLEAP, or LightningPose? I could not find these details in either this manuscript or the preprint describing AVATAR. Does the apparent performance benefit of CLOSER still apply when using standard keypoint trackers rather than AVATARnet?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important point. While the description of the characteristics and advantages of the recording system is beyond the scope of our manuscript, we are glad to introduce the AVATAR network.
AVATAR’s approach differs from standard keypoint-based methods in how the underlying data is labeled and how the final body-part locations are computed. Whereas methods like DeepLabCut, SLEAP, or LightningPose typically rely on precisely annotated keypoints—individual points placed by human annotators at the exact location of a joint—AVATAR leverages an object detection paradigm. Instead of labeling a single point, the annotators define a region corresponding to each body part (e.g., a bounding box around the hand, foot, or head). From this region, AVATAR extracts the centroid of the associated pixels to determine the body-part position.
This difference in approach yields distinct noise characteristics:
1. Labeling Consistency
For point-based systems, human annotators must pinpoint the exact joint location. Even with careful guidelines, there can be subtle inconsistencies—one labeler might place the marker slightly off-center or on a different anatomical landmark than another. This can introduce labeling noise that propagates into the trained model and its predictions. By contrast, with AVATAR’s region-based labeling, it is generally easier and more natural for annotators to consistently mark the entire area of a body part. This leads to more uniform and reliable training data, potentially reducing the variability introduced by subjective judgments about a single “correct” point.
2. Aggregation over Pixels
Keypoint-based methods provide a single coordinate per joint, making them sensitive to small deviations in that coordinate. AVATAR’s centroid estimation effectively averages over a group of pixels associated with a body part. As a result, small variations at the edges of the region or slight shifts in pose translate into more stable centroid estimates. This averaging effect can smooth out noise, reducing frame-to-frame jitter in tracked positions compared to methods that hinge on a single pixel-level determination.
3. Robustness to Annotation Errors
In a keypoint labeling scenario, a single misplacement by a few pixels can cause a noticeable change in the predicted location. In the region-based approach of AVATAR, the centroid calculation is more robust in dealing with such minor discrepancies. A slightly over- or undersized bounding box still likely captures the true location of the body part fairly accurately once the centroid is computed.
In summary, while keypoint-based models may face more noise from subtle, hard-to-control labeling differences at a single coordinate, AVATAR’s object detection and centroid-based approach can mitigate such issues by relying on more consistent and easily defined training labels. This approach, in turn, can produce more stable positional estimates and potentially lower the overall noise in the final tracked outputs.
Since CLOSER extracts the behavioral syllables from detected keypoints, we anticipate that the reviewer’s concern regarding the compatibility of CLOSER with alternative pose estimation systems could be resolved by the high sensitivity and specificity demonstrated by the AVATAR pipeline. Additionally, supplementary videos provided in the preprint (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.12.31.474634v1.supplementary-material) further illustrate the strong pose tracking accuracy of the AVATAR pipeline.
Comment 4. If the authors are going to compare KP-MoSeq and VAME with CLOSER, they should also show that CLOSER provides clear benefits in the analysis of the chronic stress model (e.g. the decoding in Fig. 3h).
Response:
We appreciate this excellent suggestion, which was also raised by another reviewer. We share the same interest and had anticipated that analyzing performance in the diagnosis of mouse depressive disorder using three different motion recognition frameworks could underscore the necessity of our tool. However, the GPU-RAM demand of VAME exceeded our computational resources due to the HMM processing on the massive dataset. Fortunately, Miller, Stephanie R., et al. recently introduced a k-means algorithm for latent space clustering, which has been shown to improve the classification accuracy of the genetic Alzheimer’s disease model (Miller, Stephanie R., et al., 2024). Building on this advancement, we used the keypoint-MoSeq and k-means version of VAME segmentation to explore the effectiveness of alternative segmentation methods in the detection of subtle behavioral changes in stressed mice.
Following the analogous approach to the examination of diagnostic accuracy shown in Figure 3h, we investigated the predictive performance of individual pipelines for depressive disorder in mice. To demonstrate this, we partitioned the motion sequences of non-stressed and stressed mice into 5-minute segments for both males and females. Behavioral syllables and summaries were then extracted employing alternative methods, which were subsequently used to train random forest classifiers for diagnosis. We have now incorporated these results in the main manuscript (Results, line 223) with a new supplementary figure 3. The relevant section and the figure are added below:
“To further evaluate the efficiency of CLOSER in depression diagnosis, we applied the same analysis on male and female groups using the syllable combinations identified by VAME and keypoint-MoSeq. Classification accuracy indicated that CLOSER outperformed VAME and keypoint-MoSeq in the male mice, achieving superior predictive performance for both classifiers trained using syllable frequency of transition (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b). In contrast, for non-stressed and stressed females, the random forest classifier leveraging syllable frequency from keypoint-MoSeq demonstrated greater performance compared to other behavior recognition pipelines (Supplementary Fig. 3c); nevertheless, the syllable transition calculated by CLOSER consistently yielded the highest accuracy (Supplementary Fig. 3d). Notably, behavioral deconstruction in males offered higher classification rates than in females for all segmentation methods, aligning with the observed sex-dimorphic alterations of syllable frequency and transition (Fig. 3i, l).”

Minor comments
Comment 1. This may just be my misunderstanding. Line 611 of the methods describes the training/test/validation split. Since the authors are analyzing data in a 10-frame window with 1 frame stride, can the same frame appear in both the training and test data? If so, the analysis needs to be repeated while accounting for any potential data leakage.
Response:
We agree with the reviewer that the same frame can appear in both the training and test datasets, as we randomly sorted the motion sequences into training, validation, and test datasets. For more details, we split those datasets to check validation loss for early stopping and to compare the loss distribution between the training and unseen datasets. However, we are confident that there is no direct information leakage from the training dataset to the test dataset for two reasons.
First, our module receives data in the form of a motion segment with a 10-frame length and, therefore, recognizes the motion in a sequence rather than a single pose (or frame). Even if the frame is repeatedly shown in different motion segments, each motion segment is distinct data, and a single frame could represent different contexts. Moreover, we mainly evaluated the quality of embedding through Linear Discriminant Analysis on the feature space instead of the test loss. Through performance evaluation of models with separate datasets, as the reviewer suggested, the data leakage problem could be solved (reviewer 2, comment 2a).
Comment 2. The writing is a bit hard to follow in places. For instance, Lines 376-379, I am not quite sure what the authors mean by the “Neuroethological nature” of their “psychomotor analysis”.
Response:
We apologize for the confusion in describing the advantages of our framework. We originally intended to inform you that the linkage between depressive disorder and psychomotor symptoms could strengthen the face validity of our diagnostic system. To clarify our statement, the text in the Discussion section (line 507) was changed as follows:
“Importantly, the neurological and molecular linkages between emotion and motor activity allow it to produce high face validity for depressive symptoms appearing in spontaneous movement.”
