Response:
We appreciate the critical feedback and hope to have addressed all concerns in our responses to the reviewer.
Major comments.
Comment 1. The authors only test one depression model (UCMS). They do not show that CLOSER is working in other models (e.g., learned helplessness, social defeat stress, chronic CORT, or genetic models like BDNF Val66Met or SERT polymorphisms).
Response:
We agree with the reviewer that further application of CLOSER-based motion analysis on different depression mouse models strengthens the power of our framework in depression diagnosis. As the reviewer suggested in the latter comment, we primarily discussed the introduction of the genetic-based depression model exemplified by the Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) Val66Met mouse line. BDNF, a neurotrophic factor playing a significant role in the survival and development of neurons, has been suggested to be related to major depressive disorder as single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the gene correlates with mood disorders. Mechanistically, the methionine substitution in BDNF leads to defective activity-dependent BDNF secretion in neural dendrites, which results in trafficking abnormality and a following increase in anxiety-related behaviors (Chen, Zhe-Yu, et al., Science, 2006). Indeed, BDNF mediates the synaptogenic and antidepressant effect of ketamine in mice (Liu, Rong-Jian, et al. Biological psychiatry, 2012). Therefore, there is no doubt that BDNF has a major role in MDD (Hashimoto, Kenji., Psychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences, 2010).
However, we would like to acknowledge several limitations in the genetic model, which may contribute to its low adoption in depressive disorder research. First, the allele frequency of the Val66Met polymorphism varies across ethnicities and sub-population groups, leading to population-specific heterogeneity. In addition, the inconsistent findings regarding the influence of polymorphisms on mood disorders, as well as widespread effects on cognition or brain morphology, suggest that both Val66Met knock-in and BDNF conditional knockout mice are more suitable for monitoring the role of BDNF in depressive disorders. (Notaras, Michael, R. Hill, and Maarten van den Buuse. Molecular Psychiatry, 2015). Most importantly, the importation and breeding of the new genetic depression mouse line (BDNF polymorphism or conditional knockout mouse) is expected to take more than six months. Given the significant time required for the establishment and stabilization of this mouse line, we decided to substitute the genetic depression model with immune system-based and hormone-based models.
We now present the comparison of behavioral structures of stress-, immune system-, and hormone-induced depression models utilizing the CLOSER platform. For the immune system-based depression model, we chose the lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation model for the onset of depressive-like behavior through acute activation of the peripheral innate immune system. In addition, we employed a mouse model of depression induced by corticosterone injection to study the effect of systemic elevation of the stress hormone. In the analysis of characteristics of spontaneous behavior across depression models, we focused on (1) the distinct and overlapping alterations in exploratory behaviors in depression mouse models and (2) the power of the CLOSER platform in the discrimination of the etiology of depression models. The results of our investigation are addressed in the Results section (line 283) and new Supplementary Figure 7:
Model-specific alterations in behavioral Syntax and architecture in depression mouse models
To explore the characteristics of spontaneous behavior across depression models, we first established depression paradigms using distinct pathological triggers. We employed two depression models: an immune system-based model through a single intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS); and a steroid hormone-based model using corticosterone administration for three weeks. Given prior reports suggesting that 1-week corticosterone does not elicit depressive phenotypes27, an additional group receiving a 1-week corticosterone injection was included to estimate the validity of the model. In the LPS-induced depression model, mice exhibited hallmark depressive-like behaviors, as evidenced by increased immobility in the FST and reduced sucrose preference (Supplementary Fig. 7a). In the corticosterone paradigm, depressive-like behaviors in TST and SPT emerged exclusively after 3 weeks of administration, with no significant alterations in the 1-week group (Supplementary Fig. 7b), in line with existing literature27.
In the first step of behavioral analysis, we evaluated syllable frequency and transition dynamics employing LDA to interrogate the broader architecture of spontaneous behaviors across these models (Supplementary Fig. 7c). While non-stressed groups and saline-treated groups, regardless of models, clustered together, chronically stressed and LPS-treated groups diverged markedly from controls in both syllable usage and bigram transitions. Interestingly, while both stress- and inflammation-induced models displayed distinct separations, their behavioral trajectories diverged in opposing directions. In contrast, corticosterone-treated mice were closely positioned with controls, suggesting comparatively modest modifications in spontaneous behavior patterns. Then, we implemented a random forest classifier to quantify the discriminability among depression models (Supplementary Fig. 7d). Consistent with LDA findings, confusion matrices indicated that CUS and LPS models were readily separable, whereas corticosterone-induced models were less distinguishable from controls.
We next applied an analysis of individual syllable contributions to unveil model-specific alterations. LPS treatment elicited marked changes in the frequency of 16 syllables, whereas corticosterone treatment affected only three, all of which were also altered in the LPS-treated model (Supplementary Fig. 7e). A subset analysis using the Venn diagram illustrated the degree of overlap across the different depression mouse models (Supplementary Fig. 7f). Of note, while six syllables were commonly altered between stress- and inflammation-induced models, the directionality of syllable changes was predominantly opposite between two models, aside from one shared cluster (cluster 2). These data suggest that frequency alterations are limited to a subset of syllables and exhibit distinct patterns depending on the etiology of depression. These results may also account for the divergent trajectories of depression models observed in the LDA (Supplementary Fig. 7c). Beyond the frequency alterations, we observed pronounced disruptions in grammatical structure, particularly in the LPS model (Supplementary Fig. 7g), and few conserved transition shifts were identified across depression models (Supplementary Fig. 7h). These findings imply that the source of depression (stress, inflammation) can be inferred based on distinctive patterns of spontaneous behavior identified in the CLOSER platform, extending beyond conventional dichotomous assessments of depressive-like behaviors.

Comment 2. They claim CLOSER can show sex-specific effects but then only include male animals when testing predictive validity with the 2 antidepressant drugs.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this weakness and agree that the sex-specific effects of antidepressants should be examined to fully describe the sex-dimorphic spontaneous behaviors in the depression model. Thus, we conducted an identical antidepressant experiment in female mice and added a new Supplementary Figure 16 to include the following result. We extended the Results section (line 462) to explain our findings for the antidepressant responsiveness of stressed female mice in terms of spontaneous behavior:
Sex-dependent behavioral fingerprints in naturalistic behavior for monoaminergic antidepressants
To elucidate sex-dependent antidepressant responsiveness and its impact on naturalistic behavior, we evaluated female mice with the same experimental paradigm previously applied to male mice using monoaminergic antidepressants. Unlike the male CUS model, female mice exhibited antidepressant efficacy exclusively in SPT and not in FST, highlighting substantial limitations in the predictive validity of traditional assays (Supplementary Fig. 11d, e).
To test if the behavioral structure identified by CLOSER could be applied to reliable discrimination of stress and antidepressant administration states within the female cohort (Supplementary Fig. 16a). Analysis based on syllable usage yielded a sensitivity of 47.22% and specificity of 82.41%, whereas classifiers leveraging transition profiles demonstrated enhanced performance, achieving sensitivity and specificity values of 61.11% and 87.04%, respectively, showing an analogous trend observed in males. Subsequent SHAP analyses elucidated antidepressant behavioral fingerprints, revealing significant sex-dependent differences (Supplementary Fig. 16b). In contrast to the rearing behaviors pivotal in males, female fingerprints predominantly featured head movements and sniffing behaviors, with cluster 22 exhibiting decreased frequencies following monoaminergic antidepressant treatment, while clusters 14 and 29 differentiated fluoxetine from imipramine (Supplementary Fig. 14c). Although cluster 4 displayed analogous antidepressant responsiveness across sexes, disparities in other syllable fingerprints underscored sex-specific differences in responses of naturalistic behavior to depressive disorders and their pharmacological interventions.
Next, we investigated drug-induced on- and off-target effects within naturalistic behavior syllables (Supplementary Fig. 16c). Chronic stress significantly altered five behavioral clusters; fluoxetine and imipramine successfully reversed three to baseline states (Supplementary Fig. 16d). Notably, off-target effects were substantially pronounced in females, with fluoxetine altering eleven syllables and imipramine influencing nineteen. Cross-sex comparisons revealed minimal overlap between male and female responses to fluoxetine (two common syllables) and none for imipramine, underscoring sexual dimorphism in behavioral responses due to divergent baseline behavioral structures post-stress induction. Moreover, fluoxetine consistently exhibited more off-target effects than imipramine across both sexes.
Finally, analysis of syllable bigram transitions revealed marked differences between female and male responses to antidepressants. Fluoxetine robustly normalized stress-induced transition modifications toward non-stressed states, whereas imipramine treatment predominantly induced off-target transitions (Supplementary Fig. 16e). In conclusion, while off-target effects on syllable usage were more evident in females, off-target transitions within syllable sequences were dominant in males, further emphasizing substantial sex-dependent variability in antidepressant pharmacodynamics.

Comment 3. They claim that CLOSER has better predictive validity than classical tests for depression but then only test drug classes that actually perform well in the classical tests too (monoaminergic drugs).
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer's constructive comment about including data on non-monoaminergic antidepressants in addition to our previously reported monoaminergic findings. We agree that evaluating these additional compounds helps address the limitations of conventional depressive-like behavior tests and further illustrates the broader applicability of the CLOSER pipeline, which enhances its potential for revealing subtle antidepressant actions. In this revised manuscript, we have integrated agmatine, scopolamine, and rapastinel into our experiments and extended the analysis to compare them directly with fluoxetine and imipramine. Specifically:
1) Experimental design and drug selection
 We added three non-monoaminergic antidepressants (agmatine, scopolamine, and rapastinel) to complement our existing monoaminergic group.
 This expanded set of compounds allowed us to investigate whether broader mechanistic classes exhibit distinct or overlapping behavioral signatures.
2) Behavioral assessment and CLOSER-based analysis
 The non-monoaminergic group was subjected to the same chronic stress paradigm and machine learning (CLOSER) pipeline used for the monoaminergic group, ensuring consistent data collection and analytical methods.
 Our approach revealed drug-specific on- and off-target effects that highlight how non-monoaminergic antidepressants differ from (or sometimes parallel) monoaminergic treatments, particularly in subtle psychomotor behaviors not captured by classical tests.
3) Comparative findings
 Results demonstrated that non-monoaminergic compounds often induce broader off-target changes than the monoaminergic group, underscoring their potentially different modes of action.
 Certain behavioral clusters remained unique to non-monoaminergic treatments, while others showed partial overlap or mirrored patterns in fluoxetine or imipramine, offering deeper insights into the heterogeneity of antidepressant effects.
We trust that including these non-monoaminergic antidepressants addresses your recommendation and provides a more comprehensive understanding of how diverse antidepressant classes influence psychomotor behavior.
Below, we share the revised Figure 5, and the main document is included in the Results section, ‘CLOSER can quantify the pharmacological effects of monoaminergic and non-monoaminergic antidepressants on psychomotor symptoms (line 398)’.

Comment 7. Also, Manifestations of psychomotor symptoms are common in patients with melancholic depression and those with psychotic features – in other words, psychomotor symptoms are not a common feature in depression. There are various forms of depression, including atypical, seasonal, melancholic, psychotic, catatonic, double depression (comorbid dysthymia), and anxious/agitated forms of depression. This limitation should be mentioned!
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the subtype-specific manifestation of psychomotor symptoms. Although it is well recognized that the psychomotor symptoms are prominent in melancholic depression, our primary aim was to demonstrate that naturalistic behavioral patterns offer a robust framework for detecting hidden alterations induced by stress, and our approach uncovers such latent features that were heterogeneous across different contexts. Psychomotor symptoms were one strong evidence for the relevance of the psychiatric state and motion pattern, with neurological linkage between the amygdala and cerebellum. In other words, we still roughly expect the potential alteration in behavioral structures of human patients for various subtypes of depression, which cannot be quantified by single motion factors such as body speed, speech tone, eye movements, or self-touching. Nonetheless, we acknowledge that their clinical relevance across the full spectrum of depressive disorders remains to be determined. In response, we have revised the Discussion section (line 566) to address this limitation, with additional references that highlight the variability in psychomotor symptoms across depression subtypes:
“For broader application of CLOSER in depression diagnosis, an action recognition efficiency and diagnostic accuracy must be validated across different species and ultimately in human patients. It is important to note, however, that the psychomotor retardation and agitation are primarily characteristic of melancholic or catatonic depression (Buyukdura, J. S., McClintock, S. M., & Croarkin, P. E., 2011) (Bennabi, D., Vandel, P., Papaxanthis, C., Pozzo, T., & Haffen, E., 2013) (Northoff, G., Koch, A., Wenke, J., Eckert, J., Böker, H., Pflug, B., & Bogerts, B., 1999), and the relationship between motion patterns and other subtypes, for example, atypical, psychotic, and seasonal depression, remains elusive (Sobin, C., & Sackeim, H., 2025). Thus, despite our results, which demonstrate that naturalistic behavioral profiles captured by CLOSER reveal distinct psychomotor signatures associated with stress, additional studies on the clinical relevance of psychomotor symptoms with the full spectrum of depressive subtypes are needed to prove the applicability of CLOSER and the translational potential of these behavioral markers in human depression diagnosis.”

Response:
We agree with the reviewer that a detailed description of the shortcomings of current depressive-like behavior tests in mice to emphasize the necessity of our framework. As the reviewer suggested, despite high predictive validity, FST has suffered from low specificity (high false positives), little construct validity, and poor effectiveness in the discovery of novel antidepressants. Indeed, in our experiment (Supplementary Figure 10), FST was extremely sensitive to the administration of antidepressants in male mice. Therefore, we have removed the term ‘predictive validity’ from our revised manuscript and, instead, emphasized the high false positive rate in drug discovery to precisely describe the imperfection of traditional behavioral tests. Below is the updated paragraph (Introduction, line 54):
“Traditionally, behavioral screening tests in rodents (e.g., the tail suspension test, forced swim test, and sucrose preference test) have been used to evaluate depressive-like symptoms, such as learned helplessness and anhedonia. Unfortunately, they show low construct validity, making them incapable of reflecting the complex psychiatric symptoms and prognoses of MDD. The highly controlled environments and oversimplified conditions used to elicit non-spontaneous behaviors in these tests have limited the development of the most common antidepressants, resulting in high false-positive rates for novel antidepressant discovery. Moreover, the over-reliance of the tests on manual scoring introduces subjectivity and inter-observer variability, further limiting the accuracy and reproducibility of depressive disorders models.”
We hope this revision provides clearer insight into the limitations of the FST for evaluating non-monoaminergic antidepressants and better addresses the reviewer’s concerns.

Comment 7. Line 209 / Suppl Fig 2d-f: estrous cycle analysis is missing here, which could explain the low correlational values that might be mentioned in the text.
Response:
We appreciate the critical feedback regarding the potential effects of the estrous cycle on female behavioral outcomes, particularly in the tests for mood disorders. However, our primary objective was to compare overall male-female differences in naturalistic and depressive-like behaviors rather than to investigate hormonal fluctuations in depth. Truly, many studies on depressive model mice do not routinely measure the estrous cycle unless they intend to explore specific hormonal mechanisms5-7. Moreover, we considered that individual differences in the baseline exploratory pattern of the mouse might have a greater influence than estrous status8, prompting us to normalize post-experimental data to the baseline of individuals.
Nevertheless, we recognize that estrous cycle fluctuations may account for lower depressive-like behaviors in TST and less distinctive features in naturalistic behaviors. Comment 8. Line 318-333: Or this means that the antidepressants didn’t work in all animals. Did you check for individual variety within your dataset? According to your classical behavioral results, you have some “non-responders” to the UCMS protocol what about the antidepressants (they should be in the extended dataset that wasn’t provided so i couldnt check)? It would be great if CLOSER could predict non-responders!
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the potential of our platform in the prediction of antidepressant responsiveness based on innate behavioral characteristics. We agree that such an approach is highly novel and holds significant potential, as it could enable the tailoring of therapeutic interventions according to individual behavioral phenotypes. However, in our study, it is challenging to strictly delineate responder and non-responder groups for antidepressants, as mice exhibited statistically significant improvements in at least one conventional depressive-like behavior following drug administration. For instance, in male mice, a significant antidepressant effect was observed in FST for both fluoxetine and imipramine (Supplementary Figure 11a), suggesting that the treatment was effective, though its impact across other behavioral assays was comparatively modest. Notably, the extent of behavioral recovery appeared to vary depending on both the class of antidepressant and the sex of the animal (Supplementary Figure 11).
One major limitation is the absence of a universally accepted guideline for categorizing drug responders versus non-responders in preclinical models. While there is a consensus on defining stress susceptibility in rodents, a similar consensus for antidepressant response classification is lacking. Although biomarker-based approaches to predict antidepressant response have been explored in humans (Leuchter, Andrew F., et al.. Current psychiatry reports, 2010), these efforts are largely aimed at distinguishing between treated and non-treated patients, rather than stratifying responders within a treated cohort.
Despite these issues, we attempted to classify the non-responders in fluoxetine- and imipramine-treated groups based on behavioral tests for depressive-like phenotypes. In our dataset, the result revealed that conventional behavioral assays performed post-antidepressant treatment failed to show a consistent correlation across tests when attempting to categorize drug-treated male mice into responder and non-responder, as illustrated below. Indeed, other groups have performed a task aimed at predicting antidepressant responsiveness, involving the ‘pre-treatment recording’ of brain activity during emotional conflict regulation and the HAMD (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale) scores in humans after antidepressant treatment (Fonzo, Gregory A., et al. Nature human behavior, 2019). In contrast, to predict spontaneous behavior-based antidepressant efficacy in our condition, an alternative experimental design is required, which extracts the behavioral structure of mice following depression induction but prior to antidepressant treatment. However, in our experimental setup, behavioral recordings were performed only after both depression induction and antidepressant administration, precluding this type of analysis.
Nonetheless, we want to point out that our current dataset does reveal the distinct effects of each antidepressant on normalizing specific subsets of altered syllables. This suggests the feasibility of a symptom-guided approach, where particular antidepressants could be selected based on the pattern of syllable alterations observed in depression models. We have now included this point in the revised Discussion section, with the potential for future studies utilizing the CLOSER framework to predict responders and non-responders based on intrinsic behavioral structures as below (line 540).
“Understanding the mechanisms by which antidepressants modulate depressive-like behaviors has traditionally centered on an ideational domain. While this has elucidated key aspects of the neurobiology of psychiatric disorders, the interpretability of data remains constrained by the divergence between rodent behavioral paradigms and self-reported human symptomatology. We resolved this limitation by benchmarking the pose estimation algorithm for human motion tracking to construct a generalizable diagnostic framework.
Our framework identified the innate efficacy of each antidepressant in restoring distinct subsets of behavioral syntax and architecture and, thus, enables a subtle assessment of antidepressant effects, including quantitative evaluations of both on- and off-target actions. This insight allows for the automated prediction of drug indications tailored to the recognized symptom clusters within heterogeneous depressive disorders, offering refined therapeutic strategies with improved predictive power. A promising direction for future studies could leverage intrinsic behavioral structure under depressive states to infer treatment responsiveness, which substantially strengthens the importance of spontaneous behavior as a determinant in prescription and potential application to clinical frameworks.”

Comment 17. 13 degrees Celsius water for 5 min?! That is a very strong stressor - shallow water exposure is what is used normally and at 24-26 degrees! (e.g. JOVE Burskin & Doron 2018), TST can be part of UCMS but is problematic here because it's also used as a readout for food/water deprivation, which is unusual in UCMS, cold exposure, and sleep deprivation as well. Response:
We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding the intensity of certain stressors in our experimental design and have accordingly revised the terminology from 'chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)' to 'chronic unpredictable stress (CUS)'. However, we strongly emphasize that there is substantial variability in the stressors employed in existing CUMS protocols, with many published studies using cold swim exposure at temperatures lower than ours (13°C) or for longer durations than 5 minutes: (i) 30 min, 8°C (Leng, Lige, et al., Neuron, 2018)9, (ii) 5 min, 8 °C (Fernandes, Joneth, and Girdhari Lal Gupta., Behavioural brain research, 2019)10, (iii) 5 min, 4 °C (Song, Qiqi, et al. Neuropharmacology, 2019)11, (iv) forced swimming in ice water at 4 °C for 5 min, hot water at 45 °C swimming for 5 min (Li, Hui, and Yaping Wang., Biochemical and biophysical research communications, 2016)12, (v) 5 min, 4 °C (Chen, Guanghui, et al.. Behavioural brain research, 2015)13, and (vi) 30 min forced swimming (Liu, Meng-Ying, et al., Nature protocols, 2018)14. Indeed, many standard CUMS protocols described in these literatures apply significantly harsher conditions than those utilized here.
Next, we recognized the similarity of the cold swim and tail pinch to the FST and TST assays, respectively, and therefore deliberately implemented distinct contexts and apparatus to differentiate these stressors from the depressive-like behavioral assessments. In detail, the cylinder for the cold swim was different in size and material from the cylinder used in FST, with different water temperatures. Likewise, the tail pinch involved holding the tail gently on a surface, with all four paws of the mouse fully supported, clearly differentiating this from the suspended posture in the TST. These procedures are not uncommon in literature9-12, and our approach maximized the unpredictability and variability of the stressors, which was our primary objective.
Regarding sleep deprivation, we utilized an apparatus with shallow water sufficient only to prevent mice from comfortably lying down but still allowing them to remain seated. Importantly, the procedure was conducted during the night, whereas mice are nocturnal animals that primarily sleep during daytime hours; thus, our sleep deprivation does not constitute a full deprivation and does not represent an excessively severe stressor. We have now described the sleep deprivation methodology in the revised manuscript (Methods, line 603):
“Chronic Unpredictable Stress (CUS) model. […] (viii) 12 h of sleep deprivation with a cylindrical pedestal (2.5 cm diameter and 3 cm height) placed on the cage floor filled with 1 cm-deep tap water to prevent sleep during the dark phase, […]”
Furthermore, we reassure the reviewer that our ethical approval process thoroughly reviewed and approved these protocols, and thus, ethical considerations are fully satisfied and not a cause for concern.
Comment 18. sucrose preference – why additional food deprivation? Normally not necessary, just take the data from your ‘habituation phase’? Does this indicate that you did not get nice results there and increased the drive via food deprivation? Please at least state if the bottles were switched in the “real test” after 12h to exclude side preference influences. sawdust? Does this mean the animals didn’t have proper bedding depth (that’s a stressor that will influence your results)
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer raising important concerns regarding our sucrose preference test (SPT) methodology. However, we would like to strongly emphasize that our experimental protocol closely follows the most widely accepted and commonly employed methods for SPT in the literature14,15, including a 24-hour testing period covering both light and dark phases, 1% sucrose concentration, and adequate adaptation to water and sucrose bottles without prior deprivation. The "food deprivation" described in our initial manuscript may have caused unintended confusion. To clarify explicitly, we did not impose any additional deprivation beyond standard methodology; rather, mice had food withheld only during the 24-hour sucrose preference measurement to ensure accurate and reliable intake assessment. Furthermore, we validated the physiological impact of this standard food-withholding period by monitoring mouse body weight before, after, and one day post-SPT. As anticipated, the animals experienced a transient reduction in weight following the test but fully recovered within one day, indicating minimal stress impact.
Regarding side preference, we agree that our previous description was incomplete and have now stated in the Methods section (line 659) that bottle positions were switched after 12 hours to eliminate potential side preference biases.
“Sucrose preference test. […] The positions of the bottles were switched after 12 hours of testing to exclude the potential effects of side preference.”
Lastly, the reviewer’s concern regarding sawdust bedding is understandable; however, the sawdust was minimally applied to detect possible bottle leakage and did not compromise the standard living conditions of mice or induce meaningful stress. Control mice, tested under identical conditions, exhibited significantly different sucrose preferences and depressive-like behaviors compared to stressed groups, further indicating that bedding depth had negligible effects on the overall well-being and behavior in our experimental condition.

Response:
We agree with the reviewer that the physical pain from the TST might affect the behavioral results in the FST. However, we wish to emphasize that the impact of tail suspension was minimal on the swimming performance. Firstly, the FST was conducted after allowing a sufficient interval (at least 4 hours) following the completion of the TST, which we have now noted in the revised manuscript (Methods, line 673):
“Forced swimming test. The forced swimming test (FST) was conducted to assess behavioral despair, at least four hours after the TST to minimize any potential effect of physical discomfort caused by tail suspension. […]”
Secondly, when removing the adhesive tape used for tail suspension, we carefully used a razor blade to minimize any possible tail injury or pain. Moreover, mice experiencing physical discomfort typically exhibit noticeable twitching or abnormal movement patterns in water; such behavioral indications were not observed in our FST video recordings. Indeed, there was a significant difference in immobility in the FST between stressed and non-stressed groups, which proves the validity of our experimental schedule.

Response:
The reviewer raised an important issue regarding the inconsistencies in sample sizes across different behavioral tests. Originally, we conducted experiments in main figure 3 on 22 male and 24 female mice. However, in the TST, several mice remained motionless, hanging onto their tail, which introduced ambiguity in determining whether such postures should be classified as immobility, since we commonly define immobility as the duration during which the mouse remains motionless with only minimal movements necessary to maintain balance. Thus, mice clinging to the tail presented a borderline scenario, and we initially decided to exclude these individuals from the TST analysis under the rationale that their hanging might not reliably reflect behavioral despair. Furthermore, as those same mice displayed depressive-like behaviors in the FST and SPT, we presumed that such exclusion would not compromise the overall dataset.
Nonetheless, we acknowledge the reviewer’s concern that this approach may cause confusion and result in nonuniform sample sizes. Therefore, we re-examined our criteria, considering relevant literature and alternative implementations such as measuring tension changes on the bar where the tail is suspended (Steru, Lucien, et al., Psychopharmacology, 1985) (Crowley, James J., et al., Neuropsychopharmacology, 2006). Based on these considerations, we concluded that it would be more consistent and transparent to include those mice in the TST result, treating the passively suspended posture as immobility. Consequently, we have reanalyzed the data and updated the corresponding figures, legends, and statistics in the manuscript to ensure uniform sample sizes across the tests. We also revised the Methods section for TST to specify our immobility criteria, explicitly stating that remaining completely motionless, whether clinging to the tail or not, is categorized as immobility (line 669):
“ Tail suspension test. […] Mice were considered immobile when hanging motionless, swinging passively, or remaining completely motionless.”

Reviewer #4
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript presents CLOSER, a self-supervised contrastive learning framework designed to analyze spontaneous rodent behavior in a chronic mild stress model of depression. This approach represents a step forward in behavior quantification by integrating 3D skeleton tracking and unsupervised learning. CLOSER provides a tool for advancing preclinical psychiatric research, particularly in identifying nuanced depressive-like behaviors and tracking responses to antidepressant treatments in a more ecologically valid setting.
Key contributions of the manuscript include the following:
First, CLOSER enhances behavior quantification by integrating 3D pose skeleton data, which captures detailed motion patterns and adds granularity to behavioral segmentation. This approach enables a more refined quantification of behavior, which is especially beneficial for nuanced analyses in psychiatric and behavioral neuroscience research.
Second, the framework leverages a self-supervised contrastive learning approach, organizing behavioral representations effectively without reliance on labeled data. While contrastive loss is common in other areas of ML it was not applied to animal behavior quantification yet.
Third, CLOSER applies its analytical power to the Chronic Mild Stress (CUS) model, identifying behavior changes associated with chronic stress in rodents and revealing sex-specific and time-dependent behavior patterns. These findings offer insights into the differential impact of chronic stress on behavior, and the model’s application to pharmacological studies demonstrates its potential for preclinical drug screening.
Finally, the model shows potential for creating standardized, reproducible behavioral assays, with the ability to quantify behavioral changes linked to both depressive-like phenotypes and antidepressant responses. This represents a promising advancement for translational research and reproducibility in animal models of psychiatric disorders.
CLOSER’s implementation builds upon the MoCo (Momentum Contrast) framework by Meta, incorporating several similar components for contrastive learning, such as a dual encoder system, momentum-based updates, and a projection head. The model architecture mirrors MoCo’s query-key structure, with two encoders to process different behavioral data modalities, stabilized by a momentum mechanism that supports consistent embeddings over time.
The originality in CLOSER lies in its domain-specific adaptations, such as using 3D skeletal and kinematic data and tailoring augmentations to the behavioral nuances of rodents. However, the modifications are incremental rather than fundamentally new: they focus on adapting MoCo’s principles to the nuances of behavior analysis rather than introducing novel learning techniques or architectural elements.
Despite these contributions, there are several points that raise questions and could benefit from further clarification or refinement.
Response:
We appreciate the constructive feedback and hope to have addressed the reviewer's concerns in our answers below.
Major comments:
Comment 1. First, while the reported accuracy increase over VAME is an improvement, it remains marginal. The absence of error bars or confidence intervals for the reported benchmarks raises questions about the robustness and generalizability of these findings, especially considering potential dataset-specific effects or stochastic variations. Including error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests would support the accuracy claims and enhance clarity regarding model generalizability across different datasets.
Response:
We appreciate this helpful suggestion that the performance assessment requires comprehensive statistics. Together with this comment, we revised the performance measurement for three behavioral recognition models (CLOSER, VAME, and keypoint-MoSeq) in an unbiased condition. In the revision process, we carefully examined the model performance by adjusting four parts of the measurement of behavior prediction accuracy1) employment of the embedding distance-based classifier, 2) introduction of independent test dataset, 3) subtle hyperparameter tuning in VAME, 4) specification of hyperparameters in CLOSER, and 5) an adaptation of PCA and UMAP embedding.
We described a detailed analysis of the performance comparison below, which is the same as the response for reviewer 2 (major comment 2).
In detail:
1) We discarded an action module using a simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP) decoder. Commonly, self-supervised learning is operated in pre-training models using encoder architectures, then fine-tuned for specific downstream tasks after the addition of decoders. Accordingly, we adopted an exemplary algorithm in the BERT framework to investigate whether the amount and quality of information in embeddings are sufficient to be decoded into action modules using a simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP), and trained a two-layer MLP with a hidden dimension size of 100 and a RELU activation function for action module prediction. However, we found that the structure of the embedding space cannot be accurately estimated in the presence of a decoder if K-means clustering or Hidden Markov Model (HMM) are performed directly on the embedding structure. Fortunately, the k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) probing exhibits a high efficiency without any distribution assumption and is a reliable indicator of downstream task performance2. Indeed, many studies have employed the k-NN classifier to assess the quality of the latent space3,4. Hence, we revised our validation, adopting the k-NN classifier in embedding space qualification throughout the study.
2) To ensure the fairness of the comparison step, we generated an independent test dataset that was never seen during the training process. Similar to the original data production, we assigned one of thirteen behavior labels in Supplementary Table 2 to each video frame for a freely moving mouse.
3) Regarding the hyperparameter tuning in the VAME framework, we listed the default and optimized hyperparameters of VAME in the table below. It must be highlighted that we modified the VAME structure to develop an optimal environment comparable to our framework. The VAME structure, which originally managed 2D skeletal input, was adjusted to receive a 3D action skeleton while complying with the ratio of hidden dimensions. Also, we reshaped the 30-frame reconstruction / 15-frame prediction training format into a 10-frame reconstruction / 5-frame prediction to compare with other methods without bias. In addition to former optimizations, we further modulated the learning rate and the number of maximum epochs in the revised manuscript, allowing us to monitor the effect of hyperparameter manipulation. The classification performance of VAME trained with two learning rates (5e-4 or 1e-3) and two maximum epochs (500 or 20) was tested.
Hyperparameters of VAME Default Optimized
Input dimension 12 27
Embedding dimension 30 108
Frame lengths for reconstruction 30 10
Frame lengths for prediction 15 5
Input normalization Yes Yes
Optimizer Adam Adam
Batch size 256 256
Learning rate 5e-4 5e-4 or 1e-3
Max epochs (patience step) 500 (50) 500 (50) or 20
The details of hyperparameters are now added to the Methods section (line 923) as follows:
“Variational Animal Motion Embedding (VAME). For the VAME, we modified the input structure to accept 3D behavioral segments as input through the extension of the number of features, from 12 to 27, and the embedding dimension, from 30-dimension to 108-dimension. In model training and inference, we adjusted the frame lengths of reconstruction and prediction methods as ten and five frames, respectively. As the variational autoencoder architecture of the VAME consists of an encoder and a decoder, each using Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), we trained the model with the given parameters for reconstruction, prediction, and KL divergence, which shows the maximal performance in behavioral classification. […]”
4) To clarify the hyperparameter information for the CLOSER pipeline, we categorized any hyperparameters used on our platform. Specifically, the momentum of a key encoder and temperature for the InfoNCE loss and distillation calculations originate from the MoCo framework, which we utilized in the CLOSER. The maximum angle for the ‘ChangeAngle’ augmentation module was determined after a comparison of linear evaluation tests for various degrees. The corresponding table is now included as Supplementary Table 3.
5) In the previous analysis, we employed a performance evaluation to assess the quality of behavior representations, excluding the segmentation step. Based on this framework, we initially believed that it was reasonable to use the 13-dimensional PCA projection of individual frames (i.e., the input to the HMM) as the behavior representation of keypoint-MoSeq in performance estimation. To account for sequential context, we concatenated 10 consecutive frames of these PCA projections to create 10-frame length behavioral segments. However, we recognize that evaluating the input of keypoint-MoSeq alone does not fully capture the motion recognition efficiency of the entire tool. To address this limitation, we now provide an alternative comparison utilizing dimensionality reduction methods (PCA and UMAP) on raw data—comprising 270-dimension vectors representing the 3D coordinates of keypoints over 10 consecutive frames—instead of the keypoint-MoSeq input. We have included the result of the performance comparison with raw pose data (270 dimensions), PCA (13 dimensions, identical to Keypoint-MoSeq input dimension), and UMAP (13 dimensions), and addressed the detailed description. Moreover, we have revised the Results section (line 150) to clarify the employment of the PCA and UMAP embedding as follows:
“[…] Since keypoint-MoSeq employs an HMM that learns transition probabilities between states, behavioral syllables IDs, and emission probabilities from a given 13-dimensional Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projection of motion sequences, we leveraged 270-dimension representation with 13-dimension PCA and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) embedding for 10-frame length behavioral segments, instead of keypoint-MoSeq. […]”
Along with the modification of the benchmarking embedding of Keypoint-MoSeq, we re-analyzed the performance of the behavioral classification across different methods. As a result, our framework exhibited the highest balanced (66%) and top-1 (55%) accuracy. Moreover, additional metrics revealed that CLOSER consistently showed strong precision, recall, and F1 scores. We have revised Figure 2c and the corresponding Results section (line 155) to reflect the updated performance metrics as follows:
“[…] In this analysis, CLOSER provided the highest balanced (66%) and top-1 accuracy, accompanied by consistently strong precision, recall, and F1 score. […]”
Fig. 2 ǀ The CLOSER framework recognized temporal and behavioral characteristics for classifying behavior segments into semantic syllables. […] c, Normalized confusion matrix (top) and associated performance metrics (bottom) showing the accuracy of k-nearest neighbor classifier based on the latent spaces of different embedding methods. The classifiers were trained on the top of the embedding spaces with an unseen manual annotation dataset to predict the behavior labels for given segments. Accumulated performance over the fivefold cross-validation is shown. The classification rate is represented in grayscale, with white for a classification rate of 1 and black for a classification rate of 0. Box plots show 25th-75th percentiles of the precision, recall, and F1 score for methods. […]
Moreover, addressing additional comments as well (Reviewer 2, Comment 1a and 1b), we have added further intrinsic evaluation of latent spaces for different embedding methods using Pearson Correlation Coefficient, which measures intra-cluster and inter-cluster, in new Supplementary Figures 1 and 2 to strengthen the validation of embedding qualities.
Comment 2. Secondly, the use of 3D skeleton data indeed enhances behavioral segmentation, yet this could likely be achieved by combining DANNCE or similar 3D tracking tools with VAME. This integration raises questions regarding the necessity of developing an entirely new model to incorporate 3D capabilities. Comparing CLOSER’s performance with a 3D-augmented VAME (i.e. running DANNCE and adding the 3D data as input to VAME) would clarify whether CLOSER’s use of contrastive learning advantages over an adaptation of existing frameworks, or if the improvement stems only by the fact that more data (3D coordinates) are fed to the model.

The reviewer is correct that the VAME version using 3D action skeleton coordinates should be tested for a fair comparison. In fact, we had already modified the VAME framework to train with 3D coordinates. We understand that the confusion may have arisen from the lack of detailed descriptions in the previous manuscript. We have addressed this point in conjunction with our response to Comment 1. We hope this explanation resolves all the concerns raised by the reviewer.
