Response:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comment and share the same interest. As reviewer 2 (major comment 3) raised the same concerns considering the comparison of depression diagnostic power, we note that the response below is identical:
We share the same interest and had anticipated that analyzing performance in the diagnosis of mouse depressive disorder using three different motion recognition frameworks could underscore the necessity of our tool. However, the GPU-RAM demand of VAME exceeded our computational resources due to the HMM processing on the massive dataset. Fortunately, Miller, Stephanie R., et al. recently introduced a k-means algorithm for latent space clustering, which has been shown to improve the classification accuracy of the genetic Alzheimer’s disease model (Miller, Stephanie R., et al., 2024). Building on this advancement, we used the keypoint-MoSeq and k-means version of VAME segmentation to explore the effectiveness of alternative segmentation methods in the detection of subtle behavioral changes in stressed mice.
Following the analogous approach to the examination of diagnostic accuracy shown in Figure 3h, we investigated the predictive performance of individual pipelines for depressive disorder in mice. To demonstrate this, we partitioned the motion sequences of non-stressed and stressed mice into 5-minute segments for both males and females. Behavioral syllables and summaries were then extracted employing alternative methods, which were subsequently used to train random forest classifiers for diagnosis. We have now incorporated these results in the main manuscript (Results, line 223) with a new Supplementary Figure 3. The relevant section and the figure are added below:
“To further evaluate the efficiency of CLOSER in depression diagnosis, we applied the same analysis on male and female groups using the syllable combinations identified by VAME and keypoint-MoSeq. Classification accuracy indicated that CLOSER outperformed VAME and keypoint-MoSeq in the male mice, achieving superior predictive performance for both classifiers trained using syllable frequency of transition (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b). In contrast, for non-stressed and stressed females, the random forest classifier leveraging syllable frequency from keypoint-MoSeq demonstrated greater performance compared to other behavior recognition pipelines (Supplementary Fig. 3c); nevertheless, the syllable transition calculated by CLOSER consistently yielded the highest accuracy (Supplementary Fig. 3d). Notably, behavioral deconstruction in males offered higher classification rates than in females for all segmentation methods, aligning with the observed sex-dimorphic alterations of syllable frequency and transition (Fig. 3i, l).”
Supplementary Fig. 3 ǀ Diagnostic accuracy of behavioral parsing pipelines in a mouse model of depressive disorder. (a, b) Confusion matrices illustrating the classification accuracy of CLOSER (left), VAME (middle), and keypoint-MoSeq (right) pipelines in male mice. The matrices compare the diagnostic performance based on syllable frequency (a) and syllable transition (b), where brighter colors along the diagonal represent a better classification rate. The CLOSER pipeline consistently outperforms VAME and keypoint-MoSeq in the male group. Box plots indicate 25th-75th percentiles of the precision, recall, and F1 score for each analytic pipeline, based on a 5-fold validation step of the random forest classifier, and all individual outcomes are displayed as data points. (c, d) Confusion matrices and box plots describing classification performance and statistics for non-stressed (CTRL) and stressed (CUS) female mice, using classifiers trained with frequency (c) and transition (d).
Comment 4. Finally, the paper does not provide a detailed comparison of the findings related to the CUS model with existing literature to establish their novelty in the neuroscience field. Without such a comparison, it's challenging to determine whether these behavioral patterns represent new discoveries in neuroscience or if they align with previously reported observations. Have there been perhaps some new substantial findings using the new method that were not known so far?
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s critical comment regarding the novelty and significance of our findings compared to existing literature. Psychomotor symptoms in humans are well-established clinical features, particularly within melancholic depression subtypes16,17. However, current mouse models predominantly rely on tests with known limitations, including low construct and predictive validity (e.g., sucrose preference test and tail suspension test), and high sensitivity but low specificity (e.g., forced swim test). This has led to the predictive validity of current preclinical drug screening using traditional mouse models remaining unsatisfactory. Indeed, recent literature pointed out a need for enhanced preclinical frameworks, which evaluate the animal behavior in semi-naturalistic settings to capture complex, ethologically relevant behaviors for high translational potential and predictive validity in drug discovery18.
To date, comprehensive machine learning-based frameworks to evaluate naturalistic behaviors across various depression models and antidepressant treatments remain unexplored. Sturman et al. (2022)19 tried to discover alterations of naturalistic behavior in the predator stress mouse model, while they didn’t estimate diagnostic performance based on their behavior profiles, in addition to limitations in comprehensive evaluations across different etiologies, pathological stages, and antidepressant efficacy. In another study, Dolensek et al. (2020)20 employed tail suspension as a sole stressor and analyzed the naturalistic behavior in this mouse model without any post-hoc investigation. Numerous studies have utilized motion characteristics to differentiate other disease states such as Parkinson’s disease21, Alzheimer’s disease22, and epilepsy23. Yet, comprehensive and high face validity models addressing chronic stress-induced depression through naturalistic behaviors and drug efficacy screening have not been established.
After thorough revision in response to reviewers’ constructive feedback, we have now significantly improved our manuscript by:
 Employment of distinct depression models: stress, inflammation, and hormone-induced models (new Supplementary Figure 7, line 283)
 Estimation of antidepressant effects on naturalistic behavior structures of female mice (new Supplementary Figure 16, line 462)
 Comparison between traditional monoaminergic antidepressants and novel non-monoaminergic antidepressant candidates (Figure 5, line 398)
 Validation of high-quality embedding in our CLOSER pipeline designed for depression diagnostics (new Supplementary Figures 1 and 2, line 117)
Based on our findings, we would like to highlight two significant discoveries of this manuscript.
1) Sex-dimorphic depressive symptoms and drug actions: Conventional depressive-like behavior tests could not illustrate differences between male and female depression models. Our naturalistic behavior analysis, however, distinctly reveals pronounced sex-dependent differences in behavioral structures and antidepressant efficacy. Considering the sex-independent drug prescription process in human depressive disorder, this finding suggests sex-dependent prognosis and underscores the incorporation of gender considerations into clinical antidepressant prescription.
2) Antidepressant-induced recovery of depressive phenotypes in naturalistic behaviors: While previous studies only emphasized general behavioral changes induced by antidepressants, our results demonstrate how antidepressants restore depression-induced alterations in behavioral structure, highlighting the capability of our framework to quantify “on-target” drug efficacy.
We acknowledge that translational relevance from mouse models to human clinical settings necessitates further validation. Nonetheless, our manuscript provides critical evidence addressing whether motion features have diagnostic value in the depression mouse model. Therefore, we think that we established a novel approach for depressive disorder and provided a strong rationale for future translation application of motion profiles in diagnosis by demonstrating heterogeneous behavioral features in the depression model mice through our depression-optimized frameworks.
Comment 5. In terms of reproducibility, while the code is available, the absence of example datasets limits the ability of other researchers to replicate the findings or to test the model on new datasets. Providing a sample dataset or detailed data specifications would allow others to reproduce the results for reviewers AND readers and evaluate CLOSER’s effectiveness across diverse datasets.
Response:
We sincerely apologize for omitting the sample datasets, including the mouse 3D coordinates used in our study. We have now uploaded the whole raw dataset at the provided Zenodo link to guarantee the utility of the CLOSER.
Minor comments.
Comment 1. The manuscript presents confusion matrices for classifier accuracy, but the interpretation of these matrices is limited without details on error patterns. This limitation restricts insights into potential misclassifications. Adding evaluation metrics like precision, recall, and F1 scores, along with error bars, could illustrate model reliability and provide a more comprehensive understanding of classification performance.
Response:
We agree with the reviewer that confusion matrices themselves cannot provide sufficient information on the classification performance. Therefore, we have added detailed classification statistics for all confusion matrices in the manuscript.
Comment 2. The use of LDA to visualize antidepressant effectiveness could be strengthened by a rationale for its selection over other dimensionality reduction techniques. Including a comparison with alternatives like t-SNE or UMAP would offer a broader perspective on clustering patterns and further support the use of LDA.
Response:
We understand the reviewer’s point about the utilization of other dimensionality reduction (DR) methods for the representation of behavioral structures to prove the effectiveness. However, our key rationale for using LDA, a supervised DR method, is to find a projection that best separates the data based on known class labels, while t-SNE and UMAP, unsupervised algorithms, cannot reflect the label of experimental samples. Given that the group labels were known in advance, we do believe that LDA was the appropriate choice to highlight group separability in the embedding space.
Nonetheless, additional visualization of behavioral structures using t-SNE and UMAP could strengthen the discriminability of CLOSER in mouse conditions. Thus, we performed t-SNE and UMAP on the dataset of Figure 3, which included behavioral syllable frequencies and transition probabilities from stressed and non-stressed male, female groups.
However, these unsupervised approaches didn’t clearly separate the groups in the reduced two-dimensional space, which indicates that although group-discriminative information exists in the higher-dimensional space, simple preservation of topological structure in 2D is not sufficient to capture these distinctions. Although these are intriguing results showing the difference of DR methods on behavioral structures, we did not include them in the revised manuscript, as we think that a comparison of various DR methods is beyond our scope, while LDA analysis is sufficient to address the structure of naturalistic behaviors in mice.
Comment 3. The robustness and interpretability of SHAP summary plots for antidepressant efficacy would benefit from both global and individual feature importance, helping to identify consistent features across different conditions. Presenting individual SHAP values for specific animals or conditions could clarify which features are universally important or context-dependent in the assessment of antidepressant efficacy.
Response:
We agree with the reviewer that highlighting individual feature importance for each drug or stress condition could enhance the distinctiveness of the behavioral fingerprint of each antidepressant. In our original manuscript, we presented impactful syllables for each drug, but we recognized the need to emphasize top-five SHAP values at both global and individual scales to better capture the distinctive features of each drug. Accordingly, following the reviewer’s comment, we have added individual SHAP plots for these top-5 impactful features in the new Supplementary Figure 14, with a detailed description of how they reflect key differences across antidepressant efficacy (Results, line 430):
“[…] Utilizing SHAP analysis for deeper behavioral profiling, we identified syllables that critically influence antidepressant classification, indicative markers reflecting antidepressant heterogeneity (Fig. 5e). Different variants of "rear up" behaviors emerged prominently as discriminative features. Specifically, increased occurrences of clusters 48, 47, and 4 and decreased cluster 3 activity characterized positive predictions for non-monoaminergic antidepressants, while inverse patterns distinguished monoaminergic treatments (Supplementary Fig. 12a). Within groups, fluctuations in cluster 19 contributed to precise drug identification. These findings underline that the CLOSER pipeline effectively leverages profound behavioral compositions of mice to distinguish psychiatric drug actions, offering potential for personalized therapeutic recommendations grounded in behavioral phenotypes.”
Supplementary Fig. 14 ǀ SHAP analysis reveals treatment-specific alterations in behavioral syllable contributions in mouse models of chronic stress and antidepressant interventions. a, SHAP summary plots of most impactful syllables for individual prediction of monoaminergic or non-monoaminergic antidepressant treatments in male mice. b, SHAP values for male mice treated with saline, fluoxetine, or imipramine in the absence of stress exposure. Each table lists the top five impactful behavioral syllables along with corresponding annotations. c, Explanation of the random forest classifier predictions for stressed female mice administered with monoaminergic antidepressants. In adjacent SHAP plots, the x-axis denotes the SHAP feature value, reflecting the magnitude and direction of each syllable’s contribution to classification outcomes. The sign of the SHAP feature value indicates the decision tendency of the classifier for a given group. Each dot represents an individual animal, with color gradients indicating the relative expression level of each behavioral syllable.
Comment 4. The interpretability of the results for drug classifications based on confusion matrices is unclear. Supplementing these matrices with precision-recall metrics or analyzing specific types of errors (e.g., false positives vs. false negatives) could offer insights into the model’s strengths and weaknesses in classifying stress conditions and drug responses. Clarifying why certain drugs or conditions are more challenging to classify would make the results more actionable.
Response:
We appreciate the suggestion for careful interpretation of the classification of drugs. Before stating the classification, we would like to inform you that we have now included non-monoaminergic antidepressants (agmatine, scopolamine, and rapastinel) in addition to previously reported monoaminergic agents (fluoxetine and imipramine) to broaden our comparison of distinct antidepressant mechanisms. Monoaminergic antidepressants target neurotransmitters such as serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine, while the non-monoaminergic compounds act through alternative pathways, for example, muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs) or N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs).
Next, following the reviewer’s suggestion on the interpretability, we investigated the false negatives of the random forest classifier by categorizing errors into three categories—vehicle, intra-group, and inter-group—thereby clarifying how naturalistic behavioral patterns differentiate drug classes. This fine-grained error analysis helped us understand the strengths and weaknesses of our model in capturing subtle distinctions between monoaminergic and non-monoaminergic effects. Moreover, we incorporated sensitivity and specificity for a qualitative assessment of the classifier’s performance following the minor Comment 6 below. We believe that these additional metrics and the expanded set of non-monoaminergic comparisons enhance the interpretability of our classification approach. We have revised our Results (line 413) and added a new Supplementary Figure 12 as follows:
“CLOSER can quantify the pharmacological effects of monoaminergic and non-monoaminergic antidepressants on psychomotor symptoms. […] As the initial step of our ML-guided behavioral evaluation, we implemented a machine learning-guided behavioral evaluation to discern subtle alterations within exploratory behaviors. A random forest classifier, informed by syllable frequencies and transitions, yielded sensitivities of 40.35% and specificities of 88.00% (Fig. 5b). Incorporating transition information enhanced performance, raising sensitivity to 50.07% and specificity to 90.01%. We examined the classification errors, which revealed predominant confusion within drug groups; however, inter-group and vehicle-associated misclassifications remained moderate (Supplementary Fig. 12).”
Supplementary Fig. 12 ǀ Distribution of false negative rate in random forest classification of vehicle, monoaminergic, and non-monoaminergic groups. False negative rates in random forest classification of drug types using syllable frequency (left) or (right) syllable transition features (right). Each stacked bar shows the proportion of false negatives due to confusion with a vehicle (gray), confusion within the same antidepressant group (intra-group; orange), or confusion between different antidepressant groups (inter-group; blue).
Comment 5. The syllable usage and transition analyses would benefit from statistical validation to support claims of generalizability. Adding statistical tests, such as permutation tests, and validating the results on additional datasets would reinforce the claims of generalizability.
Response:
We agree with the reviewer that the generalizability of our platform would benefit from statistical tests and validation on additional datasets. To clarify, all reported alterations in syllable frequency and transition within spontaneous behavior were statistically validated using either an unpaired t-test or ANOVA, followed by appropriate post-hoc tests, as addressed in the Statistics of the Methods section. Moreover, the details of these statistical methods are fully described in the figure legends and supplementary statistical data.
As the reviewer suggested, we conducted additional permutation tests on the behavioral structures of male and female mice from Figure 3. We then illustrated the result of permutation tests by labeling significant alterations in syllable frequency and transition calculated by the unpaired t-test or the permutation test below. The permutation tests yielded significance patterns similar to the original analysis, although slightly more syllables or bigrams were identified as significant alterations due to the lack of distributional assumptions. Since we have already employed the unpaired t-test as a statistical method, we decide not to include the results of permutation tests on depressive behavior analysis.
To further validate the consistency, we grouped the behavioral structures from two independent batches of male mice exposed to the chronic stressor and compared the representative variables, syllable frequency and transition. The result revealed that overall syllable distributions are similar between batch groups, and only two syllables (syllables 45 and 34) showed statistical differences. The transition bigram exhibited a few weak transition differences between the batch sets. These findings indicate that, while some minor batch-to-batch variations exist, the differences are modest relative to those observed between stress conditions.
Comment 6. The reliance on balanced accuracy as the sole metric for classifier accuracy may not fully capture the model’s performance in distinguishing depressive symptoms. Including metrics like sensitivity and specificity would offer a comprehensive evaluation and ensure that the classifier’s performance reflects accuracy across various symptom categories.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this weakness, and we strengthened the interpretation of classifier accuracy through sensitivity-specificity analysis. We have addressed this point in conjunction with our response to minor comment 4.
Detailed points (citations from the draft):
Draft: In the estimation of model prediction accuracy, the algorithm incorporating Scale, ChangeStartPoint, ChangeAngle, and ChannelMask presented the best performance for both Top-1 (73%) and balanced accuracy (70%) in the classification of manually labeled mouse behavior segments
Comment 7: This is absolutely unclear, how should the reader know what the algorithm incorporating Scale, etc, means?
Response:
We recognize that the usage of the function name can confuse readers. We have revised the terminology to intuitively represent the type of augmentations with the best performance. The changed text in the main manuscript (Results, line 111) is as follows:
“[…] In the estimation of model prediction accuracy, the algorithm incorporating size scaling, joint angle distortion, motion crop, and x- or y-axis mask presented the best performance on all evaluation metrics for the classification of manually labeled mouse behavior segments.”
Draft: To determine and categorize behavioral syllables, which are minimal motion units involving ethological context, we leveraged K-means clustering in 128 dimensions to partition behavior segments into 50 clusters.
Comment 8: How were these numbers picked?
Response:
We appreciate the insightful comment regarding the selection of the number of clusters, which was not addressed in the previous manuscript. To determine an appropriate granularity, we varied the number of clusters (from 10 to 100 in increments of 10) and investigated whether a single cluster represents a single behavioral pattern or if identical behavioral motifs split into multiple clusters. Through this evaluation and subsequent parameter tuning, we concluded that the final choice yields (50 clusters) behavioral syllable sets that are independent and unique, thereby providing an optimal balance for specificity and interpretability in our behavioral sequence embeddings.
However, we agree with the reviewer that determining the optimal number of clusters should be estimated in a quantitative manner. Here, we evaluated clustering quality using both the Silhouette score and Davies-Bouldin index across a range of cluster numbers (from 10 to 100 in increments of 10). The results indicated a general trend of improved clustering quality as the number of clusters increased. This suggests that our embedding space focuses on distinctions of fine-grained behaviors.
Although clustering performance continued to improve beyond 50 clusters, we chose 50 as a practical compromise, since it sufficiently captures the structural diversity of the ethogram. As shown in the annotation results, 50 clusters are enough to represent diverse behavioral categories. Moreover, we would like to emphasize that our software allows users to adjust the number of clusters in the k-means clustering step, which enables flexible tuning of the analysis to suit specific experimental needs.
Draft: Given the continuous nature of mouse behavior, a behavioral syllable was denoted as a consecutive frame with the same cluster label.
Comment 9: No minimum length was picked or no smoothing or filtering applied?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for spotting this issue. As the reviewer mentioned, we didn’t apply filtering or smoothing the segment according to the length, including the minimum length condition. The main reason for such an algorithm is that the distribution of frame lengths for behavior syllables calculated from a majority voting was comparable to other existing approaches, VAME and keypoint-MoSeq (Figure 2b). To provide a clearer indication of the length of identified syllables, we revised the corresponding section to include the time information in addition to the frame length (Results, line 141).
Draft: Cluster labels were determined by majority voting on a maximum of ten cluster candidates collected at the first learning step (Fig. 1a).
Comment 10: Unclear, how were the ten cluster candidates collected?
Response:
We understand the reviewer’s point and make sure to clarify the concept of dynamic temporal segmentation in Figure 1a. A central idea behind our approach is that as one frame belongs to up to 10 behavioral segments, which are obtained from a sliding window of size 10 frames with a stride of size 1 frame, we can do majority voting on cluster labels assigned to those behavioral segments. The corresponding main text (Results, line 130) is as follows:
“[…] Then, a cluster label for each frame was determined by majority voting on candidates assigned from respective sliding windows at the first learning step (Fig. 1a). Given the continuous nature of mouse behavior, a behavioral syllable was denoted as a consecutive frame with the same cluster label.”
Draft: Observing the transition of behavior motifs longer than 10 frames with z-scored keypoint change-scores, we found that the start frame
Comment 11: It would be much more scientific to report seconds/milliseconds, than the number of frames so that the reader can compare this value directly to other publications without reading up on which frame rate you were using.
Response:
We appreciate this helpful comment and have changed all texts containing frame information, including the sentence above.
Draft: ... and segments created by keypoint-MoSeq (27.93 ± 34.95 frame) but longer than those created by Variational Animal Motion Embedding (VAME) (7.75 ± 12.52 frame) ...
Comment 12: which configurations have you used for both packages?
Response:
We clarified the configuration of CLOSER in the new Supplementary Table 3. Additionally, hyperparameters used in VAME are listed in the table included in major comment 1. The table also incorporates hyperparameters used in the optimization process.
Draft: In this analysis, CLOSER provided a higher balanced accuracy (73%) than VAME (68%) or keypoint-Moseq (37%).
Comment 13: Could you provide this as +/- STD over multiple videos to see the degree of error in generalization?
Response:
To address the reviewer’s comment, we assembled an independent test set composed of mice and video sessions not used during training. We then evaluated classification performance for CLOSER, VAME, and pose representations (including PCA and UMAP) in major comment 1. These results confirm that CLOSER not only achieves the highest average accuracy but also maintains general performance across independent sessions, demonstrating its generalization to unseen data.
Draft: Initially, we performed an LDA projection for syllable frequency and transition summaries of five-minute intervals to address the sexual disparity in stress-induced ethograms (Fig. 3g).
Comment 14: So far, the LDA and transition summaries have not been introduced, hence is hard to follow here.
Response:
We apologize for the absence of an explanation for the LDA and syllable transition diagram. The Result section (line 208) was extended as below with additional citation:
“[…] Initially, we performed a Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) to transform the syllable frequency and transition summaries of five-minute intervals into a low-dimensional subspace (Fig. 3g), which enhances the expressiveness of stress-induced ethograms to address the sexual disparity (Fig. 3g). As LDA searches the axes showing the best classification performance, the larger distances between samples from different classes indicate the higher disparity in original data. […]”
Draft: In both males and females, CLOSER-identified syllables and sequences enabled the classifier to predict depressive disorder,
Comment 15: To make sure, has this been tested on unseen data?
Response:
For all confusion matrices in the main manuscript, we adjusted 5-fold validation and prepared the dataset by partitioning 20-minute sample recording videos into 5-minute sections (Methods, line 993). We adopted such a training and test set methodology to overcome the limitation of the number of behavioral datasets.
Draft: In the hierarchical structure of defined behavior syllables, clusters assigned analogous labels were located adjacent to one another in the hierarchy table
Comment 16: How come there are so many labels related to “sniff”? It seems to me that these are labels that have been randomly assigned during labeling but not a concise dictionary of behaviors defined a priori (ideally comparable to different publications).
Response:
The reviewer correctly points out the issue regarding the annotation of sniffing behaviors. In the original manuscript, we labeled “sniff” for investigations, which include both “stretched attend” and “undirected sniffing” (https://mousebehavior.org/ethogram-comparison/). To distinguish two different investigation modes, we have now revised the manuscript and corresponding figures, so that the sniffing syllables are assigned solely for undirected sniffing behavior.
Draft: …with discrete distribution patterns of behavior segments in embedding spaces for global and local components built with LatentOut.
Comment 17: What is LatentOut? Please don’t use code functions in an article, that’s really hard for the reader to interpret and make sense of if the code is not known of not of interest.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Anomaly detection is the task that identifies anomalous instances without explicit training. Among various anomaly detection algorithms, we applied LatentOut, developed by Fabrizio Angiulli, et al., which enables an anomaly detector to train on a corrupted dataset. Therefore, we confirm that LatentOut is not merely a function but an anomaly detection algorithm. However, we acknowledge that additional clarification is necessary to enhance readability and ensure that readers can follow the subsequent analysis. To address this, we rewrote the sentence with the corresponding reference (Results, line 37), which now reads:
“[…] with discrete distribution patterns of behavior segments in embedding spaces for global and local components built with latent space-based anomaly detection26 (Supplementary Fig. 3i, j).”
Draft: This finding indicated that the antidepressants only partially alleviated the depressive symptoms in spontaneous behavior.
Comment 18: It’s OK to say “indicated”, but making some judgments based on LDA embeddings is rather naive.
Response:
We recognized the inaccuracy of our interpretation and omitted the sentence from the main manuscript.
Draft: We addressed this problem by applying a self-supervised contrastive learning algorithm with augmentation modules that force the machine to embrace the underlying behavioral structure while ignoring irrelevant features
Comment 19: How do you define “irrelevant features”?
Response:
The reviewer raises an important point. In the previous manuscript, we meant to emphasize a characteristic of contrastive learning that output embeddings where similar instances are located closer in the embedding metric space (Charlotte Loh et al., 2022), and used the ‘irrelevant features’ to express factors with marginal effect on the syllable segmentation of mice (for example, the size of individuals). We acknowledge the ambiguity of terminology and have altered the text (Discussion, line 514) using technical terms:
“[…] We addressed this problem by applying a self-supervised contrastive learning algorithm with augmentation modules that force the machine to embrace the underlying behavioral structure using invariance and contrast.”
Draft: This leads to the development of transferable and generalizable ML agents
Comment 20: How is your codebase an ML agent?
Response:
We agree with the reviewer that an ML agent is only appropriate for reinforcement learning, where agents learn optimal strategies for specific tasks, and have replaced the word with ‘toolkit’ for the self-supervised algorithm.
Draft: Indeed, the algorithm generated high-quality embedding for naturalistic behavior compared to other recent unsupervised toolboxes, with clear recognition of novel motion patterns imperceptible on visual inspection.
Comment 21: How can you say that if your score was marginally better than for the competition? This needs to be re-assessed with a larger scope and at least an additional dataset in comparison.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for bringing this point to our attention. We strengthen the performance measurement including the unseen, independent dataset as mentioned above (major Comment 1). We believe that the improved analysis provides a comprehensive assessment of efficiency comparison for individual behavioral recognition toolkits.
Final Verdict
While CLOSER is a carefully implemented application of contrastive learning for analyzing rodent behavior, its contributions appear primarily incremental. The model heavily relies on the established MoCo framework, with adaptations that are domain-specific but do not introduce fundamentally new methodologies or architectural innovations. These modifications—such as using 3D skeletal data and behavior-specific augmentations—tailor MoCo’s principles to the nuances of rodent behavior analysis but lack technical novelty.
Furthermore, the manuscript does not clearly establish whether its primary contribution lies in the methodological adaptation or in producing new insights within the neuroscience of depressive behavior. Although it reports findings of sex-specific and time-dependent behavior changes in a chronic stress model, the novelty of these results for neuroscience is not convincingly discussed (hopefully this will be confirmed with reviewers with more understanding of the particular field). Without detailed comparisons with existing literature, it is challenging to assess whether these behavioral observations offer new understanding or align with previously known patterns.
For these reasons, the paper would benefit from a clearer positioning of its main contribution—whether as a novel behavioral quantification tool or a source of new biological insights—and from substantial additional justification for the technical and scientific novelty of its findings. The authors should aim to clearly establish unique methodological contributions that distinguish CLOSER from existing models like MoCo, provide detailed comparative benchmarks to demonstrate added value over simple adaptations of MoCo and strengthen generalizability through robust statistical validation.
Response:
Throughout the revision process, we have aimed to develop the manuscript into a comprehensive framework explicitly designed for depression diagnosis and drug indication through naturalistic behavior, addressing critical translational gaps in preclinical research, with demonstration of broader and stronger applicability, as described in major Comment 4. We believe that the improvements made substantially enhance the clarity in the scientific relevance of our work, in addition to methodological distinctiveness.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks on code availability):
In terms of reproducibility, while the code is available, the absence of example datasets limits the ability of other researchers to replicate the findings or to test the model on new datasets. Providing a sample dataset or detailed data specifications would allow others to reproduce the results for reviewers AND readers and evaluate CLOSER’s effectiveness across diverse datasets.
Response:
We sincerely apologize for omitting the sample datasets, including the mouse 3D coordinates used in our study. We have now uploaded the whole raw dataset at the provided Zenodo link to guarantee the utility of the CLOSER.

### Reviewer 1

In their revision, the authors have completely failed to take account of my original comment - which they agreed with - that the forced swim test and the tail suspension test do not measure depression, behavioral despair, or any other, similar anthropocentric, subjective construct. They state "We thank the reviewer for raising this important issue about the interpretation of conventional behavioral tests (FST, TST, and SPT), and fully agree that these tests have significant limitations in construct validity ...." Unfortunately, they then go on to make the contradictory and erroneous statement "yet they remain essential for validation of the depression models in mice." These tests do not have construct validity or face validity, and are therefore irrelevant for validation of valid mouse models of behavioural processes relevant to depression. For example, there is no objective evidence that swimming/climbing or not swimming/climbing during placement for a few minutes in water has anything to do with any neurobehavioural process that underlies or contributes to depression. Some antidepressants induce an acute increase in swimming/climbing behaviour, but to then misinterpret this as meaning that the mouse would have otherwise been depressed or in a state of behavioural despair is complete nonsense.
What I think the authors are trying to argue is that they are vindicated in using the FST and TST because many other groups have done so in the past and continue to do so. But to continue making the same mistake is not a basis for progress in science. At some point, authors - and editors - need to take a stand and stop using and publishing these tests.
The very least that the authors need to do in the current manuscript is to apply appropriate, objective vocabulary: this means that they need to use physical descriptions of what was observed in tests rather than nonsensical, subjective interpretations.
Therefore:
"Moreover, while FST and TST are widely used to represent behavioral despair1, we agree that these tests alone could not capture learned helplessness. Thus, we have removed the term ‘learned helplessness’ from our manuscript and replaced any use of the phrase ‘depressive symptom’ with the more precise term ‘depressive-like behavior’ or ‘depressive-like phenotypes’ to avoid overstating the clinical implications of our findings."
These tests do not represent behavioural despair and do not capture learned helplessness. Behavioural despair is such a complex emotional state it is ridiculous to infer it here. Do not use the terms behavioural despair or depressive-like; instead, state, objectively, whether one group showed less or more immobility in the test, and then state that the effect of stress was opposite to that induced by an acute dose of an antidepressant. Al least then, it will be clear that the tests were used because of their sensitivity to antidepressants, whatever this may indicate.

### Reviewer 2

I applaud the authors on the new version of the manuscript, which is significantly improved. However, two of my major concerns still need to be addressed before this is suitable for publication.
Major point 1
In the last round I was concerned that the authors did not directly validate their contrastive learning method. In response to this concern, the authors nicely show that the embedding space of data samples in the same cluster are more correlated than those assigned to different clusters. However, this does not address whether they are learning an invariant representation, this only addresses whether the clustering algorithm is working properly. In fact, a common problem in clustering animal behavior is that the same behavior can be assigned different clusters simply due to size variation. If the embedding space were highly sensitive to size, then the clustering algorithm would take, e.g., rears in small mice and rears in large mice and assign them different clusters. The inter-cluster distance would be larger than the intra-cluster distance *because the embedding space is not size invariant*. In other words, the author’s result does *not* confirm size invariance.
The more incisive analysis is in Supplementary Fig. 2, where the authors show that two clusters have strong intra-cluster correlations with mice different in weight, size, or individuality. If I understand this correctly (important detail: I could not easily find what was done here described in the legend or in the methods so please fix this). It does look like VAME and CLOSER do a better job than PCA or UMAP. However: (1) the analysis is only shown for two hand-selected behaviors, and (2) as far as I can tell the correlations are not shown for mice with matched weight, size or individuality, which would be a suitable comparison.
I recommend the following. First, explicitly plot the weights, sex and individual balances for all behaviors. If the representation is indeed invariant to these quantities you should see weights, sexes and individuals all equally represented in all clusters. Second, repeat your correlation analysis for all behaviors and you must compare different weights, sexes and individuals against the correlations with these variables matched. This will tell us how much the correlation drops as a function of weight, sex and individuality. Third, run a decoding analysis to see if you can decode weight, sex or individuality from either the embedding space, the cluster frequency, or the transition matrix. If CLOSER truly is invariant the decoding should be close to chance. At the moment the reader still cannot tell how well their contrastive learning pipeline actually performs at its stated objective.
Major point 2
I raised concerns about the scale augmentation previously. In response the authors show an example of scale being applied. Again, I am glad to see this but it does not directly address the concern. The concern is whether variation in mouse size can be explained by a single scale parameter uniformly applied to x, y, and z. Can the keypoints of a large mouse be explained by simply multiplying the x, y, and z coordinates of a smaller mouse by one number?
Here, the authors need to take the skeleton of a single example mouse and show that you can apply scale to the x, y, and z coordinates and get a reasonable match to the skeleton of another mouse different in size (and/or sex). To estimate how good the fit is, the authors can estimate a null distribution by taking the discrepancy across skeletons of mice from the same sex and size. The authors need to quantify how reasonable their approach is since it is central to the method.
Minor points
I am not expecting the authors to conduct a complete analysis of AVATAR in this manuscript, I agree it is beyond scope. That said, they are using AVATAR as the basis for all work in this manuscript and it is not standard in the field, so some description is required. Can the authors cite quantitative evidence that AVATAR provides better labeling consistency, and is more robust in localization and with respect to annotation errors as they claim in the rebuttal? Hopefully I didn't miss this, but I could not easily find direct evidence for these claims in the AVATAR preprint (at the moment the supplementary figures do not appear to be accessible). There should be enough information for the reader to have a sense for how noise characteristics, accuracy, etc. compare to standard trackers like SLEAP, DLC and Lightning Pose, and whether this could impact the results of the manuscript.
I found typos. I am listing a couple of examples here, but please thoroughly check for typos and writing clarity.
Line 757 typo (JoinJittering)
Line 923 typo (For “the” VAME)

### Reviewer 4

The authors have answered all my questions, except the following points:
Regarding comment 1 point (3):
a) The hyperparameter table for VAME notes "Max Epochs" (the maximum number of training epochs) to be 500 or 20. As VAME is a self-supervised method using RNNs, the setting of 20 seems to be far to little to guarantee convergence. Can you clarify which of the max epochs criteria was used in the results presented in the manuscript? In case you used both settings, it would be helpfull to see the confusion matrix in 2)c) to be plotted for both settings in the supplementary material.
b) the table provides a great overview of original and adapted hyperparameters. The textual version of the table that is available in the new manuscript in lines 923-930 is helpful, but does not carry all the details of the table. I would ask the authors to also add the table with original vs altered parameters for VAME and KeyPoint Moseq in the supplementary material of the manuscript and link it from the method section for interested readers.
c) Please also clarify shortly how data was fed into VAME and KeyPoint Moseq, i.e. were all time series concatenated together, then clustered together, or have you done that in batches, etc. This is also important for the readers to understand how you used those methods.
Regrading Minor comment 15:
o) As you now clarified that you have used 5-fold cross fold validation I would expect all reports on scores (f1, accuracy, ...) to be reported as mean +/- std in the whole manuscript as well as in all figures. Please make sure that this is implemented in the whole manuscript.
